ideas.title: Night Ledger: Sleep Evidence for Live-In Aides
ideas.one_liner: A camera-free $35 bedroom-door sensor kit that logs every night-time awakening of a dementia patient, giving live-in agencies court-grade proof of sleep or interruption, and a case for the second aide.
ideas.customer: Licensed home care agencies with 20-300 24-hour live-in cases, starting with Medicaid-contracted agencies in NYC, Long Island, Westchester and northern NJ. Secondary: families who employ live-in aides directly. Agencies pay.
ideas.problem: Live-in aides are paid for 13 of 24 hours. That is legal in New York only if the aide gets 8 hours of sleep, 5 of them uninterrupted, plus 3 hours for meals. A dementia patient who sundowns, wanders and needs toileting at 2am makes that fiction. The only evidence of sleep is the aide's own signed timesheet. Agencies face wage class actions and NYSDOL claims. Aides are underpaid and quit. The night, the most expensive and dangerous stretch of care, is the least measured.
ideas.solution: Two or three battery-powered motion or mmWave sensors (bedroom door, hallway, bathroom, exit door) and a hub that phones home. There is no video and no audio, because aides hate being watched and families in some states cannot legally record them. Each morning it produces a one-page Night Report: the longest uninterrupted stretch, the number of get-ups, exit-seeking events, and a one-tap aide confirmation of what was actually done. Quiet nights support the 13-hour pay. Noisy nights trigger a pay correction and build a documented case for the plan to authorize split-shift (two-aide) coverage. Families get 2am exit-seeking alerts on the same hardware.
ideas.why_now: In January 2026 a New York court reopened hundreds of shelved 24-hour-aide wage claims against NYSDOL and granted class certification (Legal Aid and NCLEJ). Federal DOL has only proposed reinstating the companionship exemption (July 2025). The 2013 rule is still the law, private rights of action are untouched, and state law in NY, NJ and CA applies regardless. Sensors, BLE and mmWave chips are now cheap enough to rent per case. The oldest boomers turn 80 this year, so live-in dementia cases are growing.
ideas.revenue_model: $79 per active live-in case per month, with the sensor kit rented and shipped. A one-time $1,500 to $3,000 wage-liability audit for agencies is the entry product. Families add-on at $29 per month for night alerts. Later, a fee for documentation packages that support split-shift authorization requests.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats the 13-hour rule as a labor-cost fight. Insiders know the same nightly record is a liability shield for the agency, proof of a heavier case that can justify two aides billed at full rate, and evidence for the aide, all at once. Nobody has built it because the buyer, the agency, has spent years preferring not to have the data. A class action changes that preference. Cameras are the wrong tool. Aides quit over them, and door-and-hallway motion data is enough.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy 40 off-the-shelf Zigbee or BLE motion sensors and a Pi or cellular hub. Write a script that emails a Night Report. Sell the audit as a service to 3 small LHCSAs in Brooklyn, Queens or Bergen County through wage-and-hour defense attorneys and home care association meetings, by offering a free 2-week pilot on their five heaviest cases. Ask two worker centers to beta test with aides and give aides their own copy of the log. The first paid pilots should come from agencies that were just sued or received a DOL inquiry.

ideas.title: Dementia Desk: Ex-Aide Call Center for Banks
ideas.one_liner: A remote call-center pod staffed by former dementia aides, taking the confused, repeat and possibly scammed callers that credit unions and utilities cannot handle.
ideas.customer: Credit unions ($200M-$3B assets), regional banks, municipal and regional utilities, and pharmacy chains' member-service teams. The compliance or member-experience officer signs. Medicare Advantage plan call centers are the second wave.
ideas.problem: Front-line agents are scored on handle time. A caller with dementia asks the same question nine times, fails the security questions, insists a dead husband is in the room, or is being coached by a scammer sitting beside them. Agents correct them, hang up or escalate. That distresses the caller, costs the institution money and produces fraud losses. Free training exists (AARP BankSafe videos), but nobody takes the hard calls.
ideas.solution: A warm-transfer line. The agent presses a button on any call that sounds impaired and a Dementia Desk specialist takes over within seconds. Specialists are ex-aides with 5-15 years in dementia care. They use the aide toolkit: join the caller's reality, don't correct, redirect, never argue about facts, and verify later with the trusted contact. They can also tell when a second voice is coaching. Each call ends with a structured note: risk flag, trusted-contact action, card freeze, callback plan. The service also hands the institution documented staff training for the Senior Safe Act.
ideas.why_now: The oldest boomers turn 80 in 2026, so vulnerable callers are rising fast. AI voice-clone scams against elders spiked in 2025-26. The Senior Safe Act (12 USC 3423) grants a bank immunity for reporting suspected exploitation only if the staff were trained and the training is documented. Home care aides are leaving the field with back injuries and low pay, and remote work at $20-24 per hour is a real second career for them.
ideas.revenue_model: $9-14 per handled contact with a $2,000 monthly minimum. A $4 per employee per year Senior Safe Act training add-on. Later, a per-account fee for a 'trusted contact enrollment' outbound program that reduces fraud losses.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The problem is not detection. Institutions already know who's confused. The problem is that nobody on the phone knows what to do next and every training video is passive. The scarce skill is de-escalating cognitively impaired adults, and the only people who have it at scale are underpaid home aides. This turns the labor supply that home care has been losing into a premium BPO product, and it gives aides a career path off their spines.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 8 ex-aides from CNA and HHA school alumni groups and caregiver Facebook groups. Write a 12-page call playbook from their own scripts. Offer two local credit unions a free 60-day pilot: agents warm-transfer any call they flag to a Google Voice line the pod answers, with a monthly report of fraud saves. Charge from month three. Ask the state credit union league to host a 30-minute 'confused caller' webinar as the lead source.

ideas.title: ARIA Watch: Aide Eyes for Alzheimer's Drug Clinics
ideas.one_liner: A 60-second daily safety check done by the home aide or family for patients on anti-amyloid drugs, flagging the subtle change that precedes brain-swelling side effects, sold to the memory clinic that prescribes them.
ideas.customer: Neurology and memory practices and infusion or injection programs running Leqembi and Kisunla. The buyer is the practice manager or program nurse coordinator. The revenue partner is the patient's home care agency.
ideas.problem: Anti-amyloid drugs carry ARIA (brain swelling or bleeding) risk, mostly caught by MRI at scheduled points. Symptoms such as headache, dizziness, vision change, new confusion or seizures often appear between scans. A person with dementia cannot report them. The infusion nurse sees the patient for two hours every two weeks and cannot judge baseline. The person who can is the aide, who sees the patient every morning and says 'she's not herself today.' Nobody asks the aide.
ideas.solution: A structured, plain-language daily check on a phone, with a voice option in the aide's language. It records a few observations against the patient's own baseline: gait, speech, new headache behavior, appetite, alertness and a free-text 'not herself'. A protocol turns 'change from baseline' into three levels: log, call the nurse today, or send to the ED. Alerts land in the clinic's inbox with a timeline. Aides get a small per-check stipend. The agency gets a revenue share. The practice gets documentation for safety programs and the patient-family peace of mind that keeps them on therapy.
ideas.why_now: The FDA approved Leqembi Iqlik, a home-administered subcutaneous starting dose, in July 2026, with launch in late August. Fewer infusion visits means fewer clinician touchpoints, while MRI-based ARIA monitoring remains. FDA-cleared blood tests are increasing the number of treated patients. CMS finalized new 2026 remote-monitoring codes for 2-15 days of data (99445) and the first 10 minutes of management (99470), making light-touch programs billable. Self-reported observations alone do not qualify for RPM, so the model pairs with a connected BP or pulse-ox device or bills through care-management routes such as CCM, PCM or GUIDE.
ideas.revenue_model: $45-65 per patient per month paid by the practice. A $10-15 per month stipend to the aide or agency comes out of that. Optional device add-on to unlock RPM billing. Later, pharma-funded real-world safety and function studies drawn from the aide-observed baseline data.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The most valuable clinical sensor for a patient who cannot self-report is the person who changes their sheets. Aide phrasing like 'not herself' or 'slower' is a better early signal than a symptom checklist the patient can't complete, and it arrives as a behavior change, not a complaint. Home care agencies have always been treated as a cost center by clinics. Here they become a data channel that clinics will pay for.
ideas.first_30_days: Talk to 10 memory clinic nurse coordinators and two infusion-center managers and ask what they do between MRIs. Build the check as a no-login web form and SMS. Recruit 3 agencies whose clients are on Leqembi or Kisunla, plus a neurologist champion. Offer a free 90-day pilot on 15 patients, with a monthly report of flags raised and calls avoided. Convert to per-patient pricing once one true early catch is documented.

ideas.title: Mother-Tongue Lifeline for Dementia Flashpoints
ideas.one_liner: On-demand live video calls where a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's first language and dialect coaches the English-speaking aide and calms the patient at bath, bedtime and exit-seeking moments.
ideas.customer: Home care agencies and PACE programs in immigrant-dense metros (NYC, LA, Miami, Chicago, Bay Area, Houston) with dementia clients whose aides do not share their language. Second: Medicaid managed long-term care and D-SNP plans. Third: families on a flat monthly plan.
ideas.problem: Bilingual and multilingual patients lose their second language as dementia advances and drift back to the language, dialect and idioms of their childhood. Agencies send whoever is available. The English-speaking aide cannot say the one calming phrase during the bath, so the bath fails, the patient panics, the aide gets hurt or quits, and the family blames the agency. Telephone interpretation lines translate literally, but a dementia patient's fragments and proverbs need to be validated, not translated. It is a communication problem, not an interpretation problem.
ideas.solution: A dedicated line, staffed on demand by trained bilingual retirees, nurses and teachers, covering the long tail: Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Toisanese, Cantonese, Polish, Russian, Uzbek, Punjabi, Tagalog, Greek, Armenian. A tablet or phone is propped where the patient can see it. The specialist speaks to the patient in dialect while coaching the aide in English in the earpiece: 'she's asking for her sister, say she is coming, then hum this song.' Sessions are 3-10 minutes at known flashpoints. Specialists are trained by aides in validation and redirection, not interpretation.
ideas.why_now: The post-war Soviet, Chinese, Caribbean and Southeast Asian immigrant cohorts who arrived in the 1960s-80s are now reaching moderate-to-severe dementia. Low-latency video is universal and cheap. AI companions such as KindredMind (voice clone of the caregiver, 12 languages, launched worldwide in May 2026) prove the demand, but they work best for mild cases and comfortable tech users. For moderate-to-severe dementia and live crises, the warm human voice in the right village dialect is the missing complement, and the agencies will pay per minute for it.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.25-1.75 per minute billed to agencies and plans, with 60-70 percent gross margin after specialist pay of about $0.45 per minute. Families get $129 per month for 20 sessions. Later, enterprise contracts with MLTC and D-SNP plans that cover the cost as a quality tool.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Patients revert not just to a language but to a specific dialect and era, for example Toisanese, not Mandarin, and the idioms of 1955. A literal interpreter is useless because what calms is tone, a lullaby, a proverb and a familiar name. The buyer is not the family but the agency, which is desperate because language mismatch is why its aides quit its hardest cases. Nobody pays interpreters for companionship, so this talent pool of bilingual retirees is unmined and cheap.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick two languages with dense local demand, for example Toisanese or Cantonese in NYC and Haitian Creole in Miami. Recruit 10 bilingual retirees through churches, senior centers and community media. Train them in a one-page validation script. Run it on WhatsApp video with no software. Call 15 small agencies serving those communities and offer 30 free minutes per case. Sign the first three at $1.50 per minute with a $300 monthly minimum.

ideas.title: Old Job Kits for Dementia Sundown Hours
ideas.one_liner: A monthly subscription of dignified, occupation-matched 'work' boxes, such as a retired bookkeeper's ledger and receipts or a retired mechanic's hardware bench, that calm sundowning better than puzzles or toys. Aides earn referral commissions.
ideas.customer: Adult children caring for a parent with moderate dementia at home (about $34-44 per month), plus adult day programs and memory care activity directors who buy in bulk. The family pays.
ideas.problem: From 4 to 7pm many dementia patients get restless, pace and get aggressive. Families use the TV, memory games or, worse, sedatives. Toys and puzzles marketed to dementia patients often insult them; they toss the plush or refuse the coloring book. What actually calms most patients is purposeful work related to the life they used to have: the retired accountant sorting receipts, the teacher grading papers, the seamstress matching buttons, the waiter folding napkins, the farmer sorting seeds.
ideas.solution: Family fills out a 3-minute 'what did they do for work?' intake. Each month a box ships with real, adult-looking, safe materials for that career. Examples are a bookkeeper's ledger, adding-machine paper, a rubber stamp and pre-sorted stacks. A teacher gets a stack of old spelling tests with a red pen and gold stars. A mechanic gets large washers and nuts on a workbench tray. Nothing sharp, small or childlike. A card gives the aide or family a 30-second 'handoff line' ('the boss needs these sorted before five'). Aides get a personal referral code and 20 percent commission.
ideas.why_now: CMS's push to reduce antipsychotic use in dementia and its GUIDE dementia care model (live since July 2024, with caregiver education and respite requirements) push practices toward cheap non-drug behavior tools. Short-form video is a free channel, since a grandfather 'clocking in' to sort receipts is deeply shareable. Families are stretched by cuts to home care hours and turn to anything that buys them a calm evening.
ideas.revenue_model: $34-44 per month subscription with quarterly rotation. Bulk B2B orders of $250 per month per adult day or memory care program. 20 percent referral commissions to aides and care managers. Upsell to 'career library' add-ons and licensed professional-uniform accessories.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The trick is not stimulation but purpose, and it must look like a real job, because anything that looks like a child's toy is rejected as an insult. Also, families ask their aide what to buy, and aides are the most trusted product recommenders in the house, yet no brand has ever paid them. Paying aides a commission creates a distribution channel no ad budget can match and quietly raises their income.
ideas.first_30_days: Build 6 career kits (bookkeeper, teacher, mechanic, seamstress, waiter, nurse) for under $18 each from restaurant-supply, office and hardware stores. Film 15 TikTok and Instagram clips with permission from families. Post in three large caregiver Facebook groups and offer 30 free kits in exchange for video testimonials. Give 20 aides referral codes. Sign up 3 local adult day centers for a $250 monthly pilot. Aim for 50 paying subscribers by day 60.

ideas.title: Legal Price Bargaining Co-ops for Salmon Fleets
ideas.one_liner: Back-office software and staff that let independent salmon boats negotiate price as one bloc under the 1934 Fishermen's Collective Marketing Act, as the Bering Sea crab fleet already does.
ideas.customer: Member-owned fishermen's associations, starting with one district of 150-400 permit holders that sells to only 1-3 buyers (a Kodiak, Chignik, Cook Inlet, Prince William Sound or Southeast group, not Bristol Bay first). The association pays us. Its dues are collected as a small settlement deduction, about 0.25-0.5% of landed value.
ideas.problem: A salmon fisherman is a price-taker. The processor posts a base price and a bonus schedule in June, the boat delivers before it knows the final price, and the retros show up months later. Bristol Bay's average ex-vessel price went from $1.03 in 2025 to $1.72 in 2026, and 2026's $260M fishery came off only 30.1M fish. Nobody on the fishing side of that swing had a seat at the table. Meanwhile most skippers believe acting together is illegal price fixing, so the bar talk about a tie-up dies every spring.
ideas.solution: A compliance-first toolkit for member-owned associations. It includes counsel-reviewed charter and bylaw templates under 15 U.S.C. 521-22 and CFEC permit verification at sign-up. Members can vote by SMS. A firewalled clean team collects member-submitted price, volume and quality data. From that it builds a formula price tied to public benchmarks (wholesale frozen sockeye quotes, roe prices, yen and euro, canned prices) plus a quality bonus schedule. We supply the negotiators, contract templates (multi-year formula price, settlement deadlines, audit rights) and dues collection through settlement deductions. The association is the bargaining party and we are the vendor, so we never bargain or set prices ourselves.
ideas.why_now: The 2025 crash and 2026 rebound showed the fleet how much money moves on one posted number. Processors now compete with loyalty and quality bonuses (for example $0.15 for RSW, $0.05 bleeding, $0.05 chilling). Bonuses are a formula, and formulas can be negotiated. Cheap e-sign, SMS voting and LLM contract review make an association nearly free to run. The crab fleet's Alaska Marketing Association proves the model works in Alaska.
ideas.revenue_model: $2-5K/month retainer per association, or 10-15% of dues. On a $260M fishery, 0.25% dues is about $650K/year, so a full-district association is a $65-100K/year account. Later add multi-association benchmarking subscriptions and negotiation-support fees tied to price gains.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The FCMA has let fishermen, not processors, bargain collectively since 1934. The fear that bargaining equals price fixing comes from the DOJ case where processors were the defendants (Pan Alaska Fisheries). Associations fail on operations, not law: no clean data, no dues collection, no fast votes, no credible fallback. Outsiders assume the fleet lacks leverage, but what it lacks is a secretary's office with software.
ideas.first_30_days: Pay an antitrust and fisheries lawyer $10-15K for a 10-page FCMA playbook. Pick one small port with a near-monopsony buyer and hold 10 harbor and Facebook-group sessions. Get 30-50 permit holders to sign a non-binding letter of intent. Run a members-only survey of what each boat was actually paid, timed for settlement season (Oct-Dec). Publish a 'your fleet vs. the benchmark' report. Aim for one association signed at a $2K/month retainer by February, before prices post in late spring.

ideas.title: Whale-Proof Alert Network for Longline Boats
ideas.one_liner: A reciprocal, location-fuzzed alert network that lets sablefish and halibut longliners warn each other about orcas and sperm whales without giving up their fishing spots.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators of IFQ longline vessels in the Gulf of Alaska, Southeast and Bering Sea (roughly several hundred boats), sold through fishermen's associations, at $600-1,500 per vessel per season. Expansion buyers are pelagic longline fleets worldwide (tuna, toothfish) that also lose fish to whales.
ideas.problem: Whales strip the gear as it comes up, and bad sets lose a double-digit percentage of the catch. The whales learn the sound of your hauler and follow the boat, and sometimes the fleet. Every skipper knows it, but sightings travel only on private VHF codes and phone calls. Reporting a whale reveals where you are fishing. The boat that 'brings the whales' gets blamed. So the fleet's best early-warning data is never pooled.
ideas.solution: An app and text-message bot that runs over Garmin inReach, Iridium or Starlink. A skipper sends a one-line report ('killer whales, 8 mi of hall X'). The system publishes only a fuzzed geohash after a delay and strips vessel identity. You can see alerts only if you report (reciprocity credits). A model adds depredation-risk scores by area, soak time, season and haul timing. A playbook covers acoustic hygiene: hauler noise, set and haul timing, gear moves. An optional hydrophone kit comes later. Anonymized data goes to researchers, associations and insurers.
ideas.why_now: Quotas are tight and sablefish and halibut prices are well below their highs, so every whale-eaten pound matters more. Satellite texting from the wheelhouse is now cheap and near-universal (Starlink, inReach). Researchers have shown that whales learn from boat acoustics, which gives the fleet a reason to trust a shared system. Fishermen have also been moving toward pots to cope with whales, which shows they will pay for anything that works.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-vessel seasonal subscription ($600-1,500), association-level enterprise licenses, and anonymized depredation data sold to research programs, regulators and insurers. Upside is global pelagic longline fleets that all have the same depredation problem.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not detection technology, it is mechanism design. Skippers guard spots and fear blame, so they share whale sightings only in private. A network that gives value only to reporters, blurs location and time, and hides identity solves that. It is a game-theory product disguised as a whale app. Whale behavior is also fleet-learned, so tracking anonymized boat signatures over time is a data asset nobody else has.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 25 skippers in Sitka, Kodiak and Homer through the longline associations. The sablefish season closes mid-November, so use the winter to run it as a manual pilot: a group text plus a spreadsheet plus a simple map, paying $100 for reports. Interview skippers about how they signal each other today. Draft the fuzzing rules with them. Sell pre-season subscriptions in Feb-Mar and go live for the March opening.

ideas.title: Crop Scouts of the Sea for Seafood Buyers
ideas.one_liner: A paid panel of working skippers and tender operators that texts in daily run, quality and delivery-limit data, sold to seafood buyers and lenders days to weeks before the market sees it.
ideas.customer: Wild-salmon importers and distributors, club-store and retail category buyers, Japanese and European trading houses, canned and frozen sockeye brokers, banks lending to processors, reinsurers and commodity funds. Each pays $10-30K/year. Panelists are paid, so fishermen are also customers of the cash flow.
ideas.problem: Bristol Bay is the source of most of the world's wild sockeye, and price went from $1.03/lb avg in 2025 (41.2M fish) to $1.72/lb in 2026 (30.1M fish). Farmed Atlantic salmon has futures and analyst coverage. Wild sockeye has neither. Buyers see ADF&G escapement and harvest counts and press releases, but not fish size, color, quality, roe, which processors are on delivery limits, tender backlogs, or which plants are paying up for fish. That information reaches the market 2-4 weeks late, after forward prices are already set.
ideas.solution: Recruit 150-300 skippers, crew and tender operators. Each sends a 60-second daily check-in (pounds per boat, average fish weight, limit status by processor, hours waiting at the tender, water temp, color and quality, weather, gear). Validate it against ADF&G counts and AIS. Publish a daily 'Fisher's Report' with the run-timing curve, quality and limit maps, and proprietary indexes, plus a weekly call with a retired skipper as analyst. Extend to Copper River, Prince William Sound, Kodiak and Southeast.
ideas.why_now: The one-year 67% swing in average price has made buyers and lenders hungry for earlier signals. Alt-data buyers already pay for crop scouts and satellite counts in other commodities. Starlink on boats makes real-time reporting possible. LLMs can clean messy text reports into structured data at almost no cost.
ideas.revenue_model: Subscriptions of $12-30K/year per company, custom data feeds at $50K+, and analyst calls. Pay panelists $150-400 per season out of 20-30% of revenue. Add other fisheries and other 'boots on the ground' sectors later.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Information in the fleet moves at VHF speed. The whole fleet knows the run is late, the fish are small, or the tenders are backed up days before any official number, and buyers treat it as noise. Skippers will happily share anonymized volume and quality data if you pay them, because it does not touch their contract terms or fishing spots. The valuable part is aggregation and a track record. Keep panelists' data separate from any confidential processor contract terms, and get securities and antitrust counsel before selling to funds.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 40 panelists from Facebook groups and associations while everyone is idle after settlements. Ask them for 2026 season logs (many keep daily notes and fish tickets). Backtest against ADF&G data and the 2026 price path, and show the panel's signals would have led the market. Send a sample '2026 in hindsight' report to 30 importers and analysts. Aim for 3 pilot subscriptions at about $5K each before the May opener.

ideas.title: Fish Settlement Audit Becoming the Fleet's Payment Rail
ideas.one_liner: Start by auditing settlement sheets against fish tickets to recover missed money, then become the split-pay rail that routes each settlement to crew, lessors, lenders and the IRS.
ideas.customer: Skippers and permit holders who pay $99 flat or 15% of any recovered amount for the audit. Crew use the shares calculator free. Later, skippers and quota lessors pay about 0.3-0.5% of settlement flow for split-pay, and lenders and CFEC-adjacent programs pay referral fees.
ideas.problem: The 'price' you're paid is a stack: base price, quality bonuses (for example $0.15 RSW, $0.05 bleeding, $0.05 chilling), loyalty or volume bonuses, post-season retros, and deductions for ice, fuel, gear advances and storage. Every processor's sheet looks different. The fisherman's own copy of the fish ticket sits in a Ziploc in the wheelhouse and never gets matched against the settlement. Nobody checks. Then the whole lump lands in one skipper's account weeks later and he has to act as the bank for crew shares, quota lease payments, loan payments, gear vendors and self-employment tax. That is where disputes, missed quarterly taxes and stiffed crew come from.
ideas.solution: Audit: photograph the settlement sheet and fish tickets, and an LLM parses pounds, price stack, bonuses and deductions, flags weight mismatches, missed quality bonuses, wrong grades and unexplained deductions, and prints a plain-English 'you were owed' letter. A crew shares calculator generates crew settlement sheets from the skipper's expense rules. Rail: once trust exists, route the settlement into a virtual account that auto-splits per signed crew share agreement, quota lease, loan payments, vendor invoices and a tax set-aside, with instant partial payments.
ideas.why_now: Final settlements for the 2026 salmon season are landing right now (Oct-Dec). Price swung from $1.03 to $1.72 in one year, so fishermen are checking. Vision LLMs can read messy sheets at near-zero cost. Banking-as-a-service and real-time payment rails make split-pay possible for a small team. Crew who waited about four years for crab disaster relief also learned that clean earnings paperwork is worth money.
ideas.revenue_model: Audit: $99 flat or 15% of recovery. Rail: 0.3-0.5% of settlement flow plus interchange and float. Later: earned-wage advances against booked settlements, lender referrals, claim-packet prep for federal disaster relief (crew earnings vaults double as the proof), and an anonymized price tape sold to buyers and lenders.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The skipper is the fleet's unlicensed bank, and nobody has both documents in one place. The audit is the trojan horse: it gets a fisherman to hand over settlement history, which is exactly the underwriting and routing data needed for the rail. The settlement sheet is a stack of price components, and the money is hidden in the parts nobody reads.
ideas.first_30_days: Post in fishermen's Facebook groups: 'free settlement check, send the sheet.' Process 100 sheets by hand plus LLM, log every error found, and turn 5-10 recoveries into case studies. Build the crew share calculator as a free viral wedge. Charge 15% of recovered amounts above $500. Start collecting the anonymized price stack by port, species and processor.

ideas.title: Peak-Window Uptime Plans for Fishing Boats
ideas.one_liner: A seasonal membership that pre-stages each boat's likely failure parts and rebuilt swap components in the harbor, provides RSW and hydraulic mechanics on call, and later adds a paid lost-peak-days cover.
ideas.customer: Bristol Bay and Prince William Sound drift and set net owners, plus seiners, who pay $2,000-4,000 per boat per season. A fleet of a few hundred boats is a $1M-plus business. Later an insurance partner underwrites the lost-time cover.
ideas.problem: Most of a boat's year is earned in about 10-14 days. With 2026's $1.72/lb, a busy boat can earn $5-15K a day at peak. Hull and machinery insurance pays for repair, never for the lost fishing days. A raw-water impeller, hydraulic hose, reel motor, fuel filter or failed RSW system takes a boat out for three days because the part is on a barge or a bush flight that's booked solid. The whole fleet breaks the same dozen components in the same ten days.
ideas.solution: Catalog the top 15-20 failure modes by engine and hydraulic setup. Stage member-funded kits in secure containers at Naknek, Dillingham, Egegik and similar harbors by June 1. Hold a rotating pool of rebuilt swap cores (injection pumps, hydraulic pumps, reel motors). Contract freelance diesel, hydraulic and RSW mechanics on retainer for guaranteed response times. Members can order from the grounds by satellite text. Phase two: verified downtime (AIS, dock check-in, mechanic log) triggers a fixed per-day payment during declared peak windows through an MGA partner.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 price rebound made every fishing day worth much more than in 2025. The fleet is aging. RSW is now paid for (about $0.15/lb bonus at some processors), yet the regional development association is funding apprentices because there aren't enough RSW technicians. Starlink lets skippers order parts and report faults from the fishing grounds.
ideas.revenue_model: Membership fees of $2-4K per boat per season, parts and swap-core margin, mechanic call-out fees, and a later per-day parametric lost-time premium shared with the underwriter.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Downtime costs are about timing, not repair. The scarce resource at peak is the right part on the right beach within hours, and nobody sells that. It works as pooled inventory: because the fleet fails predictably, a small stockpile insures hundreds of boats. Insurance pooling for parts is cheaper and faster to launch than insurance pooling for money.
ideas.first_30_days: Interview 30 skippers and mechanics at the November Pacific Marine Expo in Seattle and by phone with Naknek and Dillingham crews. Build the failure-mode parts list by engine and hydraulic setup. Pre-sell 40 memberships with $500 deposits by February. Line up two freelance mechanics and one RSW tech. Rent a container in one harbor and stage the first 40 boats' kits by June 1.

ideas.title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
ideas.one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
ideas.customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
ideas.problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
ideas.solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
ideas.why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
ideas.revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
ideas.first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.

ideas.title: Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls
ideas.one_liner: A contingency-fee service that finds and files the warranty claims on energized-but-empty data halls before OEM warranty clocks silently expire.
ideas.customer: Colocation developers, powered-shell landlords, neocloud operators and enterprise owners with phased or delayed-tenant builds, especially those with halls commissioned 6-14 months ago and not yet loaded. The owner pays a percentage of recovered value, plus an optional per-asset tracking subscription.
ideas.problem: Warranty clocks on generators, UPS systems, chillers, CRAH/CDUs, switchgear, and batteries usually start at shipment or startup, not when a tenant loads the hall. With delayed leases and mid-build AI redesigns, halls sit energized and idle for months. Many defects only show under real load (UPS capacitors, chiller compressors, wet-stacking gensets, breaker trip curves, coolant chemistry). By the time the tenant ramps, the warranty has expired. The turnover package is 50,000+ pages of PDFs that ops never reads, the punch-list deferrals are lost, and OEM maintenance records required to keep coverage valid are often missing. Nobody owns the clock.
ideas.solution: Ingest POs, OEM warranty terms, startup sheets, Cx reports, shipping documents and maintenance logs with an LLM pipeline to build a serial-number-level warranty ledger with real expiry dates and voiding conditions. Flag anything expiring within 120 days. Run a targeted load-dependent-defect inspection before expiry (thermography, oil and coolant samples, capacitor and battery checks, breaker testing). File claims, negotiate warranty start-date deferrals or extensions with the OEM while leverage still exists, and fix missing maintenance-record gaps. For new builds, sell a PO-stage clause pack that defers warranty start to beneficial occupancy.
ideas.why_now: There is a glut of speculative shells and delayed tenant handoffs. Reporting in 2026 shows close to half of planned US builds slipping, with only about a third of 2026 target capacity under active construction. That means many halls are powered, commissioned and idle. Equipment was bought at peak prices with tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs can now read messy closeout binders cheaply, which was the labor bottleneck for audits like this.
ideas.revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered value or avoided cost on claims and negotiated extensions, no fee if nothing is recovered. Optional $150-400 per asset per year tracking subscription. $15K-40K fixed-fee closeout audits for owners who want certainty. PO-stage clause-pack consulting for developers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The warranty is the only major asset on a data center balance sheet that expires silently. OEMs will defer warranty start dates at PO time, but almost no one negotiates it because the project team is fighting for delivery slots, not paperwork. After the fact, the owner's ops team inherits the docs with no idea when the clocks started. The money is in the punch-list items that were 'to be fixed later' and the load-dependent defects that only appear after the hall is finally used.
ideas.first_30_days: Find 3 owner-operators through PM and Cx network contacts with halls energized 8-11 months ago and not fully loaded. Offer a free 10-day scan of their closeout binders in exchange for a contingency agreement on any claims. Build the extraction pipeline on real binders (gensets, UPS, chillers first). Deliver a 'expiring within 90 days' hit list and file the first claims before the first invoice.

ideas.title: Grid-Code Commissioning for AI Campuses
ideas.one_liner: A test-and-certify service that validates how an AI campus behaves toward the grid (ride-through, load swings, oscillations), produces the field data transmission owners now must demand, and signs off on it.
ideas.customer: Owners of 50-500 MW computational-load sites (neoclouds, colo developers, hyperscalers' second-tier builds) that must satisfy a transmission owner's new commissioning process. Secondary: commissioning agents lacking grid-side capability who subcontract the work, and utilities that want a standard test-and-model package to accept.
ideas.problem: Traditional commissioning tests the facility against its own failures: pull the utility feed, gensets pick up, resistive load banks hold steady load. It does not test how UPS systems, rectifiers and GPU power supplies respond to voltage sags and frequency dips, or how synchronized training-job power swings interact with the grid. In July 2024 about 1,500 MW of data center load in Virginia dropped off in seconds. NERC's May 2026 Level 3 alert now calls for detailed load modeling, annual stability studies and a commissioning process for computational loads. Transmission owners have nothing to point at, owners have no test protocol, and everyone is using generic vendor models.
ideas.solution: A hardware-agnostic test package. Rent existing programmable AI-load emulators (Vertiv, PowerLoad and other liquid-cooled GPU-emulating load banks already exist), add high-speed PMU and power-quality recorders, and run a standard protocol: voltage and frequency ride-through, ramp and step-load profiles from real training traces, oscillation checks, and backup-transfer behavior under dynamic load. Deliver a PE-stamped report and an EMT/PSS/E model-validation dataset shaped for the transmission owner's interconnection group. Offer the same protocol to utilities as a certificate template. The value is the protocol, the sign-off and the model validation, not the hardware.
ideas.why_now: NERC issued a Level 3 Alert on May 4, 2026. FERC ordered NERC to file mandatory reliability standards for computational loads by Dec 31, 2026. Texas's SB 6 large-load rule is also expected by year end. The emulator hardware finally exists, but the commissioning process and accepted evidence package do not. The first owners to energize in late 2026 and 2027 will need this or wait months for the utility to sign off.
ideas.revenue_model: $150K-400K fixed fee per site (test campaign, report, model validation). $30K-80K per additional hall. Subcontract margin when working under Cx agents. Annual re-test and monitoring subscription of $40K-100K per site. Later, licensing of the protocol to utilities.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Commissioning teams are excellent at proving the facility survives a grid failure and almost blind to proving the grid survives the facility. The IST script stops at the fence line. The utility's planners are working from datasheet models that nobody has ever field-validated, and the person best placed to bridge the two (a data center Cx lead who has run a hundred pull-the-plug tests) has never talked to a transmission planner.
ideas.first_30_days: Hire or partner with 2 power-systems engineers (an EMT/protection specialist and a load-bank/field-test lead). Write a public 'reading the NERC Level 3 alert as a commissioning test plan' whitepaper. Pitch 5 commissioning agents on white-label subcontract. Line up an emulator rental partner. Offer a discounted pilot to a 20-50 MW neocloud or colo site heading for energization in the next 6 months, priced at cost in exchange for a published (anonymized) case study and a transmission owner introduction.

ideas.title: Ground-Truth Diligence for GPU-Backed Lenders
ideas.one_liner: Independent-engineer-style diligence and monthly monitoring on the part of a data center build that satellites cannot see: the last 90 days before ready-for-service.
ideas.customer: Private credit funds, banks and ABS investors lending against GPUs and neocloud contracts; insurers underwriting delay risk; AI labs and enterprises signing take-or-pay capacity who need to know if the promised RFS date is credible.
ideas.problem: GPU-backed loans and offtake contracts are priced on a ready-for-service date. Satellite vendors (SynMax and Industrial Info Resources now cover 2,600+ projects weekly) can show steel, cooling towers and generator yards, but they cannot see the failure zone: utility permission to energize, MV switchgear energization, Level 4/5 commissioning and IST results, liquid-cooling flush and pressure tests, fiber-plant acceptance, OEM startup-tech availability. Percent complete on pay applications is front-loaded and misleading. Meanwhile GPUs costing millions per rack sit idle and depreciate while interest accrues, and lenders are capping neocloud exposure. Traditional IEs are power-plant-oriented, slow and expensive.
ideas.solution: A 'Readiness Ladder' of about 40 binary, evidence-backed milestones (utility energization letter, gear serials and bills of lading, Cx level sign-offs, IST pass/fail counts, CDU flush logs, open-punch burn-down rate, OEM startup-tech calendar). Score each project and re-score monthly. Output a probability of RFS by date and covenant or draw-release triggers. Staff it with a bench of ex-data-center PMs and Cx leads who do desk review plus quick site visits. Sell as a 2-week second-opinion product first, then monthly monitoring, integrating vendor satellite feeds as an input rather than competing with them.
ideas.why_now: Neocloud credit risk is now the topic. Lenders are capping exposure, deals are stalling on credit risk, and GPU-debt structures (including vendor backstops) are proliferating. Analyses show roughly 40% of AI data center sites with possible delays and about half of 2026 capacity slipping, while operators publicly deny it. Satellite monitoring has commoditized the exterior, which makes the interior truth the scarce and valuable part.
ideas.revenue_model: $25K fixed-fee 2-week second opinions; $40K-120K full pre-close diligence; $8K-20K/month per facility monitoring; optional success-based fee for delay-risk insurance placement. Adjacent product: retained RFS-credibility scoring for AI labs choosing between capacity offers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Percent complete is the wrong metric. The last 5% of a data center can consume 25% of the calendar, and it is dominated by unbounded tasks: the commissioning punch-list burn-down rate and whether the OEM has a startup technician free that month predict RFS far better than construction progress. You can only read those signals if you have run an IST. Also, the RFS date on a marketing sheet is a sales number, not a schedule.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 6 retired or between-jobs Cx leads and PMs on 1099 contracts. Publish a free 'RFS credibility checklist' and a teardown of one publicly delayed project. Approach 5-10 private credit and infrastructure funds with data center or GPU-lending desks. Offer a fixed-fee $25K second opinion on one live deal, delivered in two weeks, and ask permission to reference the engagement anonymously.

ideas.title: Pull-the-Plug Testing for Hospitals and Water Plants
ideas.one_liner: Bring data center-grade full-facility blackout testing to hospitals, water utilities and other critical facilities that never actually pull the plug, and help them source scarce backup gear the AI build-out has hoarded.
ideas.customer: Critical-access and rural hospitals, water and wastewater districts, 911 centers, cold-chain warehouses and municipal facilities. Secondary payers: property insurers, hospital captives and risk pools that can subsidize tests or discount premiums for certified resilience.
ideas.problem: Routine emergency-power testing is usually a short, partial-load generator run. It rarely exercises the whole chain (utility loss, ATS transfer, sequenced load pickup, cooling, fuel supply, paralleling controls) under real load, so the interaction failures show up during the actual storm or grid event. At the same time the AI build-out has swallowed generator, switchgear and transformer production, with multi-year lead times, so a failed generator or breaker at a small hospital cannot be replaced quickly. Facility managers know their fragile points but have no credible way to test them or to find spares.
ideas.solution: A one-day 'controlled blackout' service using data center IST discipline: written sequence-of-operations script, load-bank top-up to real facility load, thermographic and breaker health checks before and after, a witnessed utility-loss transfer, fuel/cooling/ventilation checks, and a punch list. Deliver a resilience certificate with prioritized fixes and remaining-life estimates. Upsell: source and retest certified pre-owned generators, ATS and switchgear from cancelled or paused data center orders, and keep a small regional spares pool for members of a hospital or water-district cooperative.
ideas.why_now: AI infrastructure is consuming electrical gear supply (transformer lead times of 3-5 years, switchgear reportedly sold out into 2028) while nearly half of planned 2026 US data center builds are delayed or canceled, which leaves stranded but scarce gear. Storm and grid-stress events are also raising the stakes for small critical facilities. Insurers are scrutinizing resilience, and rural facilities cannot afford the big-firm engineering studies.
ideas.revenue_model: $18K-45K per facility test; annual re-test contracts; 10-15% sourcing margin on certified pre-owned gear; insurer or captive partnership fees per policyholder tested; small monthly membership for spares-pool access.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In a data center nobody trusts backup power until someone has pulled the plug at full load, and most first tests find something. The rest of critical infrastructure, which arguably matters more, almost never does this because the fear of a failed test outweighs the fear of a failed emergency. A Cx lead who has run hundreds of pull-the-plug tests can make the test routine and safe. The AI boom also turns the spare-gear problem into a secondary market that only someone who has seen the cancellations firsthand can source from.
ideas.first_30_days: Rent a 500 kW-1 MW load bank and partner with an electrical contractor. Call 10 facility directors at critical-access hospitals and rural water districts through state hospital and rural water associations. Offer 2 discounted first tests in exchange for case studies and insurer introductions. Approach one regional property insurer or hospital captive with a loss-prevention pilot. Start a private list of sellers of surplus gensets and switchgear from paused data center projects.

ideas.title: Lender-Required Benefit Records for F&I Add-Ons
ideas.one_liner: A 20-second, VIN-aware 'did this product actually benefit this buyer' check and signed record that indirect lenders demand as a funding stip, because California's CARS Act (SB 766) bans add-ons that provide no benefit and lenders inherit the exposure.
ideas.customer: Primary payer: credit unions and banks that buy indirect auto paper in California (dealer-management and compliance teams). Secondary: California franchised and independent dealer groups, at about $149 per store per month, when a lender tells them to use it.
ideas.problem: SB 766 becomes operative Oct 1, 2026. It bars charging for an add-on the buyer would not benefit from, requires clear disclosure that add-ons are optional, and requires dealers to keep records for two years. Lenders that buy the contracts carry Holder Rule and Rees-Levering exposure for what happens in the F&I office. Nobody outside the dealership can see whether GAP was sold to a buyer with 35% down, a 7-year service contract to a buyer with 6 years of factory powertrain warranty left, or prepaid oil changes to an EV buyer. The FTC's federal CARS Rule was vacated in January 2025, so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement, and the April 2026 $78.1M Lindsay Automotive settlement shows the size of the downside.
ideas.solution: A lightweight web form and API that the F&I manager fills in per product during the menu. It auto-decodes the VIN (EV or hybrid, remaining factory warranty, tire type, key type). It pulls loan-to-value from the deal numbers and runs benefit rules per product, such as GAP with LTV under about 90%, a service contract that overlaps the factory warranty, maintenance on an EV, and key replacement on a keyless-start car. It flags mismatches, captures a one-tap 'customer chose this anyway, here's why' rationale, and outputs a timestamped PDF and JSON record. Lenders add it to their funding-package checklist. The rule library is the product and is updated per state as CARS-style bills spread.
ideas.why_now: SB 766 takes effect in three days (Oct 1, 2026). Federal rule-making is dead, so the compliance burden has moved to states and to lenders' third-party-risk teams. More states are copying California's language. The Lindsay $78.1M settlement in April 2026 made every dealer compliance director and every credit union counsel pay attention.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-funded-contract fee of $2 to $4 paid by the lender or passed to the dealer, or a $149 per store per month dealer subscription. Later, sell state-by-state rule packs and an anonymized benefit-mismatch benchmark to lenders and dealer insurers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Most dealer violations are not lies. They are menu autopilot. The DMS menu shows the same five products on every deal and the pay plan rewards penetration, so a mismatch happens without anyone deciding to deceive. The buyer who will pay for compliance is not the dealer, whose incentive is to sell. It is the lender, who holds the paper, gets sued alongside the dealer, and has the leverage to make a data field mandatory at funding.
ideas.first_30_days: Read the SB 766 text and the FTC's vacated rule for the exact 'no benefit' examples, and turn them into 25 to 30 explicit rules. Build a plain web form with no DMS integration. Cold-pitch compliance officers at 15 California credit unions with big indirect books through the CUNA/California credit union compliance channels. Offer a free 60-day pilot in which they require it from their 3 to 5 highest-volume dealers. Pre-sell 10 dealers at $99 per month using the line 'your lender is going to ask for this.'

ideas.title: Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return
ideas.one_liner: A per-return concierge that unwinds a cancelled used-car deal (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales tax, commissions) inside California's new 48-hour refund deadline. It then turns the return data into a return-risk pool.
ideas.customer: California used-car dealers, especially independents and BHPH lots that sell 30 to 200 used cars a month and have no back-office bench. They pay $195 to $250 per return, or a standby retainer. Later, insurers and MGAs buy the underwriting data.
ideas.problem: From Oct 1, 2026, SB 766 gives buyers a 3-day right to cancel a used vehicle priced at $50,000 or less. Within 48 hours of cancellation the dealer must cancel the contract and refund the buyer, less only the deductions the law allows for mileage and damage. That is easy to write and very hard to do. The cost of an unwind is the cascade, not the car. The dealer has to reach the lender that has funded or is holding the contract, cancel each service contract and GAP with its administrator, and charge back the F&I commission. It also has to reverse the title, registration and sales tax, refund the down payment and any trade, and document the vehicle condition to justify any deduction. Independents have never done this at volume, and one botched unwind creates a refund violation and a private-plaintiff claim.
ideas.solution: Unwind-as-a-service. The dealer forwards the cancellation notice. The desk runs a checklist workflow that notifies the lender, submits cancellations to administrators with the correct pro-rata or full-refund basis, prepares the DMV and tax reversals, calculates the refund and permitted deductions, and produces a compliance file that meets the two-year retention rule. A delivery-day photo and video capture link is bundled, because permitted deductions depend on condition documentation. After 6 months of volume, the desk holds the only dataset on return rates, timing and loss per return in a mandatory-return regime. That data is enough to price a per-unit return-risk cover (roughly $60 to $120 per used unit) through a licensed MGA or insurer partner.
ideas.why_now: The law takes effect Oct 1, 2026, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has had a mandatory 3-day return on used cars at this scale. The 2025 to 2026 run of subprime stress, roughly 30% of trade-ins underwater and repossessions at about 3M a year, means many buyers will discover mid-week that they can't afford the payment. That is the buyer most likely to use the cancellation right.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat fee per processed return ($195 to $250). Standby retainer of about $99 per month per store for priority handling. Phase 2: 10 to 20% of premium as an MGA on the return-risk pool. Phase 3: license the cancellation-cascade workflow to DMS and eContract vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody knows the real return rate. Everyone models it on Carvana's 7-day return, but the buyers who return are not typical, because the F&I office sees payment shock and buyer's remorse first. A 48-hour refund deadline is shorter than the time a lender, administrator or DMV normally takes to process anything, so the dealer's exposure is process failure, not vehicle depreciation. Whoever owns the process owns the data, and the data is what makes the insurance product priceable.
ideas.first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist by state and by lender for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents. Sell a $99 per month standby plan with a guaranteed 24-hour turnaround per return. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a shared spreadsheet and e-sign before writing any software. Log every step's time and dollar cost, since that log becomes the actuarial dataset.

ideas.title: Payoff-Triggered Refund Recovery for Credit Unions
ideas.one_liner: A payoff-desk plug-in that finds the unearned GAP and service-contract refunds the moment a member pays off, and applies unearned add-on credits in repossession deficiencies. It goes through lenders, not SEO, so it reaches the borrowers the consumer refund sites can't.
ideas.customer: Credit unions and regional auto lenders (payoff and collections departments). The lender pays a small SaaS fee or takes a share of recovered money. Second wedge: consumer bankruptcy and debt-defense attorneys and legal aid, at $99 per deficiency audit.
ideas.problem: When a borrower pays off early, trades in, or has the car totaled or repossessed, they are owed the unearned pro-rata part of GAP, service contracts and other financed add-ons. Refunds are not automatic. Not the dealer, not the lender and not the administrator processes them, and consumer-refund sites exist because so few people claim. The incentives point the wrong way. The dealer suffers a commission chargeback, so it stalls. The administrator profits from non-cancellation. The lender never owned the product. The borrower doesn't know. In repossession, unearned add-on credits should reduce the deficiency the borrower is sued for, and they rarely appear on deficiency notices. Roughly 3M repossessions a year and subprime 60+ day delinquency at a 32-year record of 6.9% in January 2026 make this a very large pool of missed money.
ideas.solution: Ingest the closed-loan document image or loan tape, read the itemized products and financed amounts from the retail installment contract, and match each to its administrator. Compute the pro-rata or earned-basis refund by state rule (New Jersey, for example, requires an automatic refund within 60 days). Auto-generate the cancellation packet with the lender's payoff letter, odometer statement, signature or letter of authority, and the state statute citation, then track it to payment. Stalled cases escalate to the state insurance department with a complaint file. The moat is a database of roughly 60 administrators' actual cancellation requirements and response behavior, plus the 50-state rule set. The repossession product reconciles deficiency notices against the same data and outputs an attorney-ready exhibit.
ideas.why_now: Record delinquencies and about 3M repossessions a year, roughly 84-month loans with about 30% of trade-ins underwater, and long terms mean most loans die early and carry stacked add-ons. Credit unions are under member-experience and fee-optics pressure, and California's SB 766 now requires dealers to keep refund and cancellation records. LLMs can finally read messy contract images and cancellation forms cheaply enough to run at scale.
ideas.revenue_model: Credit union pays $3 to $6 per payoff processed, or 20 to 30% of recovered money with no upfront fee. Attorneys pay $99 per deficiency audit or a $499 per month subscription. Later, sell aggregated administrator refund-speed benchmarks to dealer groups and regulators.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The consumer refund sites that exist all have the same weakness: they wait for the borrower to show up. The one moment every party knows the loan ended is the payoff, and the lender's payoff desk is the only place that sees all of them. The refund itself comes from the administrator's pool, and the dealer's chargeback is a fight between the dealer and the administrator. The borrower's claim doesn't depend on the dealer cooperating, so the dealer stalling does not need to hold up the refund.
ideas.first_30_days: Build the administrator playbook for the 20 largest GAP and service-contract administrators and the 10 highest-population states. Offer 3 credit unions a free retrospective audit of 500 payoffs from the last 12 months and show them the dollar total of unclaimed refunds. Take a 30% success fee on live recoveries. Simultaneously give 5 consumer bankruptcy attorneys the repossession deficiency audit free on their next 3 cases in return for case studies.

ideas.title: Dealer-Fee Decoder for Solar and Home Loans
ideas.one_liner: Use the auto F&I trick of hiding the buy-down in the price to expose the hidden 'dealer fee' inside 0% and low-rate solar, HVAC and roofing loans, then sell the evidence to consumer lawyers and the refinance to credit unions.
ideas.customer: First: consumer-protection and TILA law firms and legal aid running home-improvement and solar loan cases, at $49 to $149 per decoded loan. Second: credit unions and community banks that pay $150 to $300 per funded takeout loan.
ideas.problem: A '0% for 12 months' or '2.99% for 20 years' home-improvement loan is not cheap. The lender charges the contractor a discount or 'dealer fee' that commonly runs into double digits on promotional-rate loans, and the contractor recovers it by inflating the price for financed customers. It's the same mechanic as a dealer's reserve and buy-down in an auto F&I office. The borrower sees a low APR, cannot see the cash price they should have been quoted, and often pays a financed price 15 to 30% above the cash price. Minnesota's attorney general has sued GoodLeap over hidden fees folded into loan amounts, and complaints keep growing. Homeowners left with orphaned systems and no tax credit are a sympathetic and litigable group.
ideas.solution: A document-parsing decoder. The homeowner or lawyer uploads the contract, TILA disclosure and any competing cash quote. The tool extracts price, APR, term and any disclosed fee, and estimates the implied cash price and implied finance charge, meaning how much of the price is really interest. It compares this to a regional cash-price benchmark built from scraped quotes, contractor bid sites and permit data. It outputs a plain-language one-pager and a lawyer-grade exhibit for TILA and UDAP claims, then offers a credit-union takeout quote for the true payoff amount.
ideas.why_now: The federal residential solar tax credit for homeowner purchases ended after 2025, a wave of installers went bankrupt and left homeowners with loans on systems nobody services, state attorneys general have started suing, and the CFPB's federal enforcement has faded so states and private plaintiffs are the enforcement. Contingency-fee plaintiff firms are already advertising for GoodLeap-type cases and need faster intake screening.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-case fee from law firms ($49 to $149), a subscription for high-volume firms ($499 per month), and a bounty from credit unions for each funded refinance or takeout loan. Later, a compliance benchmark sold to honest contractors, to lenders and to regulators.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Consumer advocates attack solar lenders as if the fee were unique to solar. A finance manager knows it is standard structure anywhere a merchant can 'buy down' a rate: the retail price quietly carries the cost. What law firms lack is not the theory but cheap, defensible, per-loan numbers to screen thousands of leads. The cash price counterfactual is the missing piece and the F&I mindset is exactly what tells you where to look for it.
ideas.first_30_days: Collect 200 real solar and HVAC loan document sets and cash-vs-financed quote pairs from public complaints, forums and two or three law-firm partners. Build the parser and implied-price model on them. Offer three plaintiff firms with active solar-loan intake 25 free screens each, then charge $99 a case. Meet two credit unions with home-improvement loan programs to agree a bounty for takeouts.

ideas.title: Sold-Out-of-Trust Radar for Floorplan Lenders
ideas.one_liner: Catch dealers that sell floored cars and pocket the payoff by watching the one signal an F&I insider knows can't be hidden: the VIN disappears from public listings but the floorplan payoff never arrives.
ideas.customer: Floorplan lenders and their auditors: independent floorplan companies, captive finance arms, regional banks and credit unions with dealer lines, and warehouse lenders that fund subprime and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Pay $15 to $30 per monitored dealer per month plus enterprise data fees.
ideas.problem: A dealer sells out of trust when it sells a floored car and does not pay the lender's payoff on time. It is how small cash squeezes become fraud. Ford and Stellantis are in court against Sky Auto Mall over exactly this, and floorplan use is heavier with inventory at roughly 88 days' supply and rates at SOFR plus 200 to 400 bps. Lenders police it with periodic on-site audits (monthly, quarterly or random), so a dealer can sell for weeks before anyone looks. The dealer's own delay makes it worse, since contracts in transit stretch to a week or more before the lender funds, so honest and dishonest dealers look identical in the books.
ideas.solution: Daily VIN-level monitoring of each lender's floored inventory against public and licensed listing feeds from the dealer's site and the major marketplaces. When a floored VIN disappears from listings, the tool starts a clock. It cross-checks against lender-provided payoff events and, where available, title and registration transactions and electronic lien releases. If no payoff shows within the expected window (about 7 to 10 days for a clean deal, longer for slow lenders), it flags the dealer and VIN and ranks risk by dealer history and how many VINs are in the queue. Flags trigger a spot audit or a curtailment call. A dealer-facing version shows honest dealers exactly which VINs look 'unpaid' so they can fix processing before the lender calls, and it doubles as an early-warning feed for warehouse lenders.
ideas.why_now: Sept 2025's Tricolor and PrimaLend collapses put double-pledged collateral and verification failures in front of every subprime lender and their investors. In March 2026 Ford and Stellantis were still litigating floorplan fraud against Sky Auto Mall. Rising inventory and higher rates increase floorplan reliance. Public listing feeds and cheap LLM data extraction make VIN-level monitoring practical for a team of three.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-dealer monthly monitoring fee, a per-alert fee on confirmed cases, and enterprise data licensing to captives and ABS or warehouse investors. Upsell: a contracts-in-transit tracker that gives dealers a lender-verified funding timeline and later powers same-day advances against verified contracts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The only place SOT cannot hide is the retail listing. A dealer will lie about payoffs, backdate titles and pay one lender with another's money, but it still has to take a car off its website when it sells it, because customers and marketplaces punish stale listings. Auditors check what is on the lot; nobody checks what left the internet. An F&I person knows this from watching sold cars vanish from the site the same day the deal is signed, and from knowing how long a funded payoff should really take.
ideas.first_30_days: Build a scraper for a pilot set of 50 dealer inventory pages and a listing-history log. Backtest on cases visible in public court filings (the Sky Auto Mall filings and a handful of others) to show the signal would have fired weeks earlier. Approach three small independent floorplan lenders and two credit unions with dealer floorplan lines, offer a free 60-day pilot on their books, and charge $20 per dealer per month after proving at least one real catch.

ideas.title: Cash Advances Against Steam Payouts
ideas.one_liner: A receivables-and-ad-float lender for live Steam games, underwritten from the studio's own Steamworks wishlist and sales data instead of the game's quality.
ideas.customer: Steam-live indie studios and micro-publishers with roughly $50k-$1M a year in net Steam revenue and 100+ reviews. They pay a flat fee of about 8-12% on each advance, repaid from Steam payouts.
ideas.problem: Valve pays about 30 days after month-end, so a launch-week spike reaches the bank up to two months later. In that gap the studio sees ads producing wishlists at a profit (say $1-2 per wishlist, with 15-25% converting to first-week sales) but has no cash to scale the spend, pay for a console port or fund localization. Indie Fund and new funds like Blue Ocean's $30M (2026) back development, not post-launch receivables. Banks treat games as hit-driven lotteries.
ideas.solution: A 'Payout Bridge'. The studio connects a read-only Steamworks financial and wishlist key. We forecast net receipts for the next 60-90 days from launch-day wishlists, demo conversion, regional mix and refund rate. We advance 30-50% of that forecast, or pay ad platforms and streamers directly as an 'ad float'. The studio points its Steam payout to a sweep account so repayment comes off the top. A free 'Steam funnel benchmark' dashboard built on the same keys is the top of the funnel and the data moat.
ideas.why_now: Steam gets roughly 20k releases a year, so marketing spend, not development, is now the main cost and the main cash-flow gap. Small funds are proving capital appetite for indies in 2026. Steam Machine (June 2026) and Steam Frame (Sept 2026) are widening the PC base. LLM tooling makes per-game underwriting cheap enough for $10-40k tickets.
ideas.revenue_model: A flat 8-12% fee on each advance, 60-120 day terms, with a fee premium for the ad-float product. Later: a subscription for the benchmark dashboard, and a securitized pool sold to a credit fund.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A lender doesn't need the right tail that VCs obsess over. The first 30 days of Steam sales track launch-day wishlists within a fairly tight band, and Valve is a reliable payer. So credit risk is behavioural (the studio changing its bank details) and can be solved with a sweep account, not with taste in games. Underwrite the wishlist funnel and ignore game quality.
ideas.first_30_days: Ship the free Steamworks-key benchmark dashboard and seed it in Steam dev Discords, r/gamedev and the wishlist-marketing newsletters. Raise a $150-250k first-loss pool from angels or a small credit line. Manually underwrite 5-10 advances of $10-40k for studios that just launched or have a Next Fest spike. Get a fintech lawyer to structure it as a purchase of receivables.

ideas.title: Contingency Royalty Audits for Game Developers
ideas.one_liner: A $99 automated statement check that finds provable underpayments in publisher royalty reports, then hands winnable cases to forensic accountants on contingency.
ideas.customer: Developers signed with publishers who are unrecouped or getting opaque quarterly statements. They pay $99-299 for the check and 20-25% of any recovered money. Referral fees also come from games lawyers and auditors.
ideas.problem: Audit clauses exist in most publishing deals (one analysis found them in 88% of deals with an advance), but a formal audit costs more than a small studio can recover, so publishers effectively face none. One 30-contract analysis found 42% gave the publisher 100% of revenue until recoupment. Marketing 'recoupables', vague net-revenue definitions, cross-collateralization and FX and VAT handling all hide errors. Devs sit on a spreadsheet they can't verify.
ideas.solution: Devs upload the contract and statements. We rebuild the recoup waterfall from the contract's own definitions and compare it with independent signals: review-count unit estimates, price history and regional mix. We flag anomalies such as marketing above a cap, taxes deducted twice, giveaway keys counted as spend, and FX gaps. A clause pack and a negotiation script push new deals toward Steamworks read-only financial permission for the dev. Flagged cases go to a panel of forensic accountants who send a formal audit notice.
ideas.why_now: The 2023-25 layoffs pushed thousands of devs into 'marketing-only' publishing deals with recoup terms. LLMs can now parse contracts and statements at near-zero marginal cost. Funding is tight, so every unpaid royalty matters.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat pre-audit fee, 20-25% contingency on recoveries (cheaper than the roughly 40% litigation contingency), and referral fees from lawyers. Later: a paid tier for funds and lenders that want portfolio royalty monitoring.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Detection was never the bottleneck. Cost was. A cheap pre-audit that separates provable errors from noise lets an auditor take only winnable cases. Publishers in a small, gossipy industry often settle quickly once a credible notice lands, because they don't want the precedent to spread, and many errors are honest spreadsheet mistakes.
ideas.first_30_days: Launch a free recoup-waterfall calculator and a 'publisher-deal red-flag scan' on r/gamedev and dev Discords. Collect about 100 anonymized statements as training and proof data. Sign referral deals with two games-industry lawyers and one forensic accountant. Take the first 5 contingency cases with flagged anomalies over $10k.

ideas.title: Preflight Lab for Steam Frame Verified
ideas.one_liner: A shared hardware lab that runs your build on real Steam Frame, Steam Machine and Deck units, finds why it would fail Valve's compatibility review, and fixes it.
ideas.customer: Back-catalog publishers with 20-200 older titles, and mid-size indie studios that want the 'Great on Frame' or Steam Machine badge. They pay $250-1,500 per title for preflight plus fix, or $1-3k a month for catalog coverage.
ideas.problem: The Steam Frame is an ARM device that runs x86 games through FEX and Proton, and it launched in mid-September 2026. Only about 131 titles were Verified at launch out of tens of thousands. Valve's review is a queue with terse pass/fail notes, and each resubmission costs weeks. Failures are usually boring: launcher windows, first-run dialogs, 32-bit dependencies, cutscene codecs, kernel anti-cheat, controller glyphs, unreadable text, missing the 30fps at 720p floor. Devs can't justify buying a $1,059 headset to test.
ideas.solution: A rack of real devices with an automated runner. It launches the build through Steam, drives it with synthetic controller input, and records frame-times. It OCRs UI text height, uses a vision model to catch launcher and dialog windows, and checks the checklist Valve publishes. The output is a ranked punch-list. A paid fix-it tier handles launch options, Steam Input configs, codec swaps and small patches, then resubmits to Valve.
ideas.why_now: Steam Machine (June 29, 2026) and Steam Frame (September 2026) just shipped, with FEX and the verified-badge process brand new. The first 6-12 months of a new Valve platform are when badges are scarce and the store gives them the most weight, as happened with Deck Verified in 2022. Back-catalog publishers will want to opt in whole catalogs at once.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-title preflight and fix fees, catalog subscriptions for publishers, and a success-based 'Verified or partial refund' premium tier.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The failures repeat across titles, so a publisher with 60 games amortizes every fix, and a lab that has fixed one FMV codec problem fixes it for a hundred games. Studios also can't afford the hardware, so shared capex becomes their opex. Triage by expected Frame-owner overlap, because the badge only pays off in genres that owners actually buy.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy 2 Frames, 1 Machine and 1 Deck (about $3.5-4k). Run 10 free preflights for devs recruited from Steam Frame and Deck communities and Linux gaming press. Publish 'the top 10 reasons Frame review fails', drawn from those real runs. Pitch 5 ports and back-catalog publishers a fixed price per title for a 20-title pilot.

ideas.title: AI Provenance Audits for Game IP Deals
ideas.one_liner: Due-diligence audits, plus a signed process-capture plugin, that tell publishers and acquirers what in a game is verifiably human-made and what IP they actually own.
ideas.customer: Small and mid publishers, game aggregators and acquirers, and lenders (idea 1's future competitors). Festival and award organizers pay for finalist verification. They pay $1.5-6k per audit. Studios and freelance artists pay $0-199 for the evidence pack.
ideas.problem: Steam's AI disclosure is self-attested. In January 2026 the form was narrowed to player-facing generative content. About one in five store listings now disclose AI use, and players punish undisclosed use, including refund fights over late disclosure. The US Copyright Office position is that purely AI-generated material isn't copyrightable, so a publisher buying a game with heavy AI art owns thinner IP than the price assumes. Awards bodies have reversed honors after discovering AI use.
ideas.solution: Two parts.
