First, a local plugin set (Aseprite, Krita, Blender, Photoshop, plus git and Perforce hooks, and C2PA where available) writes a tamper-evident, timestamped hash chain of authoring events, with no screen recording. Second, an audit desk takes a shipped build and repo and produces an asset-by-asset provenance map: evidenced human, AI-assisted, or unknown. It adds a Steam-disclosure recommendation and a copyrightability memo prepared with counsel.
ideas.why_now: Valve's January 2026 form rewrite left studios unsure what counts. AI use is now mainstream (roughly 20% of listings) and controversial. Awards and festivals are getting burned. Publishers are adding AI warranties to contracts and want a way to verify them.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-audit fees, bulk pricing for publishers with catalogs, a per-finalist fee for festivals and awards, and a paid studio subscription for evidence-pack export. Artists get the credential free, which builds the network.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Classifiers run on shipped assets are unreliable, and false positives on human artists are reputational poison. The only defensible evidence is process metadata captured at creation, which is nearly impossible to reconstruct afterward. So the buyer is the balance-sheet buyer who cares about IP ownership, not the player. Freelancers who want a 'verified human' credential to win commissions pull the tool into studios from below.
ideas.first_30_days: Hand-sell audits: contact 30 small publishers and aggregators, and do 3 discounted audits by reading source-control history and interviewing the team. Ship a minimal Aseprite or Krita plus git capture plugin. Pitch two indie festivals or awards on verifying their finalists. Publish an anonymized 'what audits usually find' write-up.

ideas.title: Licensed Cozy Games for Memory Care
ideas.one_liner: A turnkey activity program for senior living made of commercially licensed cozy indie games, in a kiosk kit that logs resident participation for compliance paperwork.
ideas.customer: Activity directors and operators of memory care, assisted living and skilled nursing communities, starting with independents and small regional chains of 5-50 sites. They pay about $199-349 a month per community plus a $349-499 kit.
ideas.problem: Nursing homes must run person-centered activity programs and document participation (CMS F-tag 679). Directors are short on budget and staff time. Existing tech is expensive proprietary hardware such as projector tables or VR. Consumer games are the wrong fit: their licences forbid commercial and public use, and they have reading-heavy UI, timers and fail states.
ideas.solution: A curated library of 30-50 indie titles that are gentle by design: no fail states, no timers, big targets, little text, familiar themes like gardening, cooking and tidying. Developers grant commercial, DRM-free licences for a revenue share. Each title runs in a locked kiosk launcher on a docked handheld or mini-PC to the TV, with big-button controllers. Staff get 5-minute group-play cards and a one-tap participation log that exports to activity documentation. It is positioned as activity programming, not therapy, so it makes no clinical claims.
ideas.why_now: About 4M Americans turn 65 each year through 2027, so demand for senior activities is rising. Handheld PCs are cheap and reliable. Senior living operators are already piloting games (for example the Belmont Village pilot of a cognitive game). Steam's glut of cozy games means many strong titles with dormant back-catalogs that earn nothing.
ideas.revenue_model: Monthly subscription per community, a hardware kit margin, and 40-50% of subscription revenue paid to developers by playtime. Later: enterprise contracts with chains, and reimbursement or wellness-budget channels.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Steam keys are personal-use licences. Only the developer can grant commercial or public-performance rights, and a dormant catalog makes them say yes for a small guarantee. The traits that make cozy games sell are exactly what dementia-friendly design needs. And directors buy relief from documentation and set-up time, not cognitive outcomes. VCs file this under 'brain-training edtech', while an insider sees a licensing arbitrage plus a compliance workflow.
ideas.first_30_days: License 8-10 cozy titles, offering $500 minimum guarantees plus revenue share. Assemble 5 kits at about $400 each. Offer free 4-week pilots to 5 local communities through activity-director Facebook groups and state activity-professional associations. Log participation minutes per resident. Convert pilots to paid at week 5.

ideas.title: Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases
ideas.one_liner: White-label filing infrastructure that lets solo immigration lawyers file mandamus/APA delay lawsuits in 48 hours, turning the government's habit of mooting suits into a flat-fee product.
ideas.customer: Solo and small immigration firms (1-10 attorneys) who pay a per-filing platform fee; end clients (naturalization, green card and employment petition applicants) pay the firm a flat $2.5-5k. Secondary buyer: employers with stuck petitions.
ideas.problem: Cases are stuck well past posted processing times: interviewed N-400s never scheduled for oath, I-485s and I-140s idling, and holds or pauses applied to nationals of dozens of countries since late 2025. Clients wait 12-30 months. Lawyers know a federal delay suit often shakes a case loose, but most solos have never filed one. Drafting the complaint, civil cover sheet, summons, service on the U.S. Attorney's civil process clerk, the Attorney General and the agency, and district-specific local rules is a 6-10 hour learning curve, and no one wants to be the first to file.
ideas.solution: A web tool with three parts. (1) An eligibility screen: enter the receipt date, form type and field office, and it compares them to posted times and to real observed outcomes, then scores the delay claim. (2) A complaint and exhibit generator with a per-district rules library, a service-of-process checklist and deadline calendar (the 60-day government answer window), and a template for the joint status report or stipulated dismissal that follows adjudication. (3) A docket-outcome database that logs, by district, judge and case type, how long from filing to adjudication. The attorney of record signs every filing. The platform is software, not a law firm.
ideas.why_now: Through late 2025 and 2026 USCIS added enhanced vetting, holds and pauses on benefit requests tied to nationality, expanded re-review of approved cases, and slower naturalization and green card scheduling. The volume of genuinely stuck cases is at a decade high. Federal courts are also less deferential to agencies since the Loper Bright decision, and adjudicating a stuck case is cheaper for the government than defending it. Solos are overloaded and short of billable-hour alternatives, so a ready-made product for a high-ticket service is easy to sell.
ideas.revenue_model: $350-600 per filing charged to the law firm (flat, not a percentage, to avoid fee-splitting rules), or $299/month for up to 3 filings. Later: a paid intelligence tier of docket-outcome analytics by district, and a litigation-funding partnership for clients who can't front the fee.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit is rarely litigated to judgment. The U.S. Attorney's Office usually tells USCIS to adjudicate within 30-90 days so the suit can be dismissed as moot, so the client's real purchase is a forced deadline. Clients almost never hear about this because form-prep firms earn on the application, not on pressure. Posted processing times are also misleading (they reflect only completed cases at a percentile), so whoever accumulates real time-to-decision data by field office and district owns the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 5 immigration attorneys in high-volume districts (N.D. Cal., S.D. Tex., D.N.J., E.D.N.Y., S.D. Fla.) and offer free templates for the first filing. Build the intake screen and three complaint templates first (delayed N-400 after interview, delayed I-485, delayed I-130/I-140 or a nationality hold). Concierge-run 10 filings by hand, charging the firms $400 each. Log every outcome date, since that dataset is the product. Post outcome stats to immigration-lawyer Facebook groups and AILA chapter listservs to pull in the next 30 firms.

ideas.title: Presence Ledger: Reconstruct Every Trip You Took
ideas.one_liner: Ingests flight emails, CBP I-94 history, location exports and passport stamps to produce an evidence-backed, officer-proof travel table for naturalization, green-card retention and tax residency.
ideas.customer: Immigration law firms (per-client fee), CPAs and tax preparers serving foreign nationals (Form 8843/substantial presence test), HR mobility teams, and green card holders or naturalization applicants directly.
ideas.problem: N-400 applicants must list every trip of 24 hours or more in the past 5 years with exact dates. Almost no one can. Officers compare the list with CBP entry and exit records, and an honest gap or mismatch turns an interview into a good-moral-character or false-testimony problem. Green card holders with long absences risk a presumption of broken continuous residence, and scrutiny of returning residents at ports of entry has risen. The same reconstruction is needed for IRS substantial presence day counts, state tax residency audits, and Schengen/UK day counts. Paralegals spend 1-3 hours per client pulling this together by hand, and it is still wrong.
ideas.solution: A consent-based tool that pulls the official CBP I-94 travel history, scans Gmail/Outlook for airline and hotel confirmations, ingests Google Timeline or phone location exports and card transactions, and OCRs photos of passport stamps. It reconciles them into a single timeline with confidence flags, asks the user only about unresolved gaps, and exports (a) an N-400-style trip table with the proof behind each row, (b) day counts for physical presence, substantial presence and Schengen limits, and (c) a warning when a planned trip would cross a risk threshold (for example 180 days, or a trip that would break continuous residence).
ideas.why_now: Naturalization is being scrutinized more heavily in 2025-26, with a new civics test, a renewed focus on good moral character and reinstated neighborhood-style inquiries. Border stops of returning residents are up. Remote and hybrid work has multiplied cross-border days and tax exposure. Location data is now easy to export from phones, and LLMs make email and stamp parsing cheap enough for a small team to build in weeks.
ideas.revenue_model: $49-79 per case billed to law firms (white-label), $29-49 self-serve for applicants, $12-20 per client for CPAs during tax season, and a $9/month subscription for green card holders who want ongoing day tracking and pre-trip risk checks.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The danger is not the trips you forget but the mismatch between your list and what the government already holds. A trip table with attached proof, pre-reconciled against CBP's own record, changes the tone of an interview. The exact same dataset is what tax audits and residency disputes need, so an immigration wedge opens a much larger tax-residency market with no extra data collection.
ideas.first_30_days: Build only the N-400 5-year trip table with I-94 history import plus email parsing. Give it free to 10 immigration firms in exchange for a testimonial and a comparison against their manual tables. Charge $49 from client number 11 on. Post the before/after error rates from real cases. In parallel, offer a $15 8843/substantial-presence day-count report through 5 CPAs who serve OPT/H-1B clients.

ideas.title: Status-Cliff Benefit Sold Through PEOs
ideas.one_liner: A confidential, employer-paid benefit that screens temporary-status workers for alternate immigration relief, tracks work-authorization cliffs, and pre-arranges counsel and family plans before a raid, TPS termination or EAD lapse hits.
ideas.customer: Payroll, PEO and staffing firms serving labor-intensive employers (home health, poultry and meat processing, hospitality, warehousing, construction, agriculture), plus the employers themselves. They pay $4-9 per employee per month or $60-120 per screened worker.
ideas.problem: Employers with workers on TPS, humanitarian parole, pending asylum EADs or DACA are losing headcount unpredictably. Terminations of TPS and parole programs hit hundreds of thousands of workers with little warning, and automatic EAD extensions ended for renewals filed after late October 2025, so employees now fall out of I-9 validity while renewals are pending. Worksite enforcement and I-9 Notices of Inspection (3 business days to respond) are rising. HR treats it as a compliance chore, then loses 10-30% of a shift overnight.
ideas.solution: A benefit package in four parts. (1) A dashboard that projects the work-authorization cliff by employee category and date, with I-9 reverification scripts that avoid discriminatory over-documentation. (2) Confidential relief screening done by a licensed partner attorney for each willing employee (family petitions, pending asylum, U/T visas, SIJS, cancellation, adjustment eligibility) with the employee, not the employer, as the client. (3) An emergency file for each participating worker: signed G-28 on file, memorized A-number card, standby guardianship documents for children, and a hotline for the first 72 hours after a detention. (4) An I-9 pre-audit and a 72-hour Notice of Inspection response playbook.
ideas.why_now: TPS and parole terminations, the end of EAD automatic extensions, expanded enforcement, and increased I-9 audits all converged in late 2025 through 2026. Employers can no longer treat immigration compliance as an annual checkbox, and existing I-9 software only tracks expiry dates. It offers no relief screening, no emergency response, and no employee-side counsel.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-employee-per-month benefit fee split between the platform and partner law firms (structured as payment to the firm for services rendered, with the third-party-payor consent required by the professional conduct rules), plus per-screening fees and a premium I-9 audit-defense add-on. PEOs and payroll firms get a distribution margin.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The employer's real loss is churn, not fines. In screenings, a surprisingly large share of workers, often a quarter or more in my experience, have a path they never knew about, because no one ever asked in a confidential setting. A worker who is told they have a path stays loyal to the employer that offered it. The right buyer is the PEO's benefits desk, since PEOs already sell legal-plan and EAP riders through one procurement decision.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one vertical (home health agencies, where TPS and parole terminations are hitting staffing hardest) and one state. Partner with 2 immigration firms that have screening capacity. Pitch 3 regional agencies and 1 PEO with a 60-day pilot: 100 employees screened for $6,000, delivered as a de-identified summary of how many have alternate paths. Use the pilot data (headcount saved, cases opened) as the sales deck for the PEO channel.

ideas.title: O-1 Evidence Vault as a Startup Employee Benefit
ideas.one_liner: Continuously captures, verifies and time-stamps the evidence that O-1A, EB-1A and NIW petitions are actually won on, so a lawyer can file in weeks instead of scrambling for six months.
ideas.customer: Venture-backed startups and AI labs with foreign-born staff pay $25-40 per employee per month. Founders, PhD students and researchers can use a self-serve tier. Immigration firms license a white-label version.
ideas.problem: The $100k fee on new H-1B petitions for workers abroad, and a wage-weighted lottery for everyone else, have pushed tech employers toward O-1A, EB-1A and NIW as the primary route. But these are evidence-driven cases. Clients show up with nothing organized, the lawyer spends weeks chasing citation counts, salary comparisons, press links and reference letters, letters end up as boilerplate, and half the evidence (paid associations, vanity press, generic membership) gets discounted by adjudicators at the final-merits stage anyway. AI-generated petitions are now a recognizable genre officers discount.
ideas.solution: A vault that connects to sources people already have (OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, GitHub/Hugging Face adoption, patents, OpenReview and conference reviewer rosters, Wayback-archived press, compensation data with consent) and adds structured quarterly manager memos documenting the employee's critical role. It logs each independent-expert letter request with dates and independence facts. Output is a criterion-by-criterion evidence map with gaps and a plain-language six-month plan, plus a flag for evidence types officers typically discount. It hands the packet to any immigration lawyer, including the employer's existing counsel.
ideas.why_now: The H-1B fee and lottery weighting since late 2025 have made O-1A and EB-1A a mainstream path rather than an exception for founders and stars. AI labs and startups need it for dozens of employees at once, so time-to-file matters. Public scholarly and code metadata are now available through open APIs, and LLMs make it feasible to structure messy evidence at low cost.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-employee SaaS ($25-40 per month), a $300-500 one-time evidence audit, and a licensing fee from law firms. Immigration counsel remains separate, and no fee-splitting occurs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Petitions are decided on what was already documented by the time the client met the lawyer. Nobody builds evidence continuously because no one owns the job: HR doesn't know the criteria, lawyers only engage after the decision to file, and employees don't know what counts. Separately, the evidence that counts (independent judging, real citations, critical-role documentation) is often free to collect early and impossible to fabricate later, while the paid pay-to-play tactics sold to nervous applicants are actively harmful.
ideas.first_30_days: Find 3 seed or Series A AI startups with heavily foreign-born teams, through their immigration counsel or investor platform teams. Run a manual concierge audit for 20 employees at $300 each, producing the criterion-by-criterion map in a spreadsheet plus Google Doc. Identify the top 5 recurring evidence gaps (they will be the same across companies) and automate those first. Convert the startups to a subscription once the first two employees file petitions faster than expected.

ideas.title: Civil-Document Runners for Immigrant Families
ideas.one_liner: A vetted in-country network that retrieves, verifies and delivers birth, marriage, police and court records for consular and NVC cases, with chain-of-custody proof and no forged shortcuts.
ideas.customer: Immigration law firms and family-based petitioners (largely South Asian, Filipino, West African and Latin American communities) who pay $150-450 per document, plus rush fees and bundled certified translation and apostille.
ideas.problem: Applicants wait on USCIS, but the delays that lawyers dread most sit at the National Visa Center and consulate: 'documentarily qualified' rejections, requests for secondary evidence, and 221(g) refusals for a missing or irregular civil document. Every country issues records differently, and the State Department's reciprocity schedule is only a starting point. Families hire fixers or relatives, sometimes receive forged or improperly obtained records, and then face a permanent fraud bar (INA 212(a)(6)(C)). Lawyers keep private lists of trusted runners abroad. They cannot scale and are not available to families without counsel.
ideas.solution: A managed marketplace of vetted local partners (lawyers, licensed document agents, registry liaisons) in 8-10 high-volume corridors (India, Philippines, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nigeria, Vietnam, El Salvador, Haiti). Each order starts with a pre-check against the consulate's actual document list, then a tracked retrieval from the issuing office with receipt and photo proof, an 'authenticity file' documenting exactly how the record was obtained, and delivery bundled with certified translation, apostille where applicable, and secondary-evidence packets when a record truly doesn't exist. Use online registries (India DigiLocker, Philippines PSA, Mexico's online actas) wherever possible so that most orders need little or no physical runner.
ideas.why_now: Consular processing has become slower and more discretionary, with more document-authenticity scrutiny, more public-charge-related evidence demands, and periodic pauses or holds by nationality. Errors that used to cost weeks now cost months. Many civil registries have digitized since 2020, so remote retrieval is now feasible for a meaningful share of documents, which makes a thin-margin logistics business viable for a small team.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-document fee ($150-450 depending on country and rush), roughly 40-50% gross margin after local partner costs, plus bundled translation and apostille, and a subscription tier for firms that order 20 or more documents a month.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody thinks of immigration as a logistics problem, so VCs fund form software while the real bottleneck is a birth certificate in a district registry that doesn't respond to email. The valuable asset is not software but a scorecard of which local partners and registry offices actually deliver on time and produce documents consulates accept. Reliability data by country and office can be built only by handling volume, and that is a moat lawyers already acknowledge privately.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick three corridors (Philippines, Mexico, India) where much of the retrieval can be done through official online portals plus one local partner. Sign 2 partners per corridor and pilot with 5 family-immigration firms at a flat price per document. Handle every order by hand, log time-to-delivery and rejection rates by office, and publish a country-by-country reliability guide to attract the next firms.

ideas.title: Alpha-Gal-Safe Pharmacy With Verified Ingredient Sourcing
ideas.one_liner: A cash-pay pharmacy and lookup service that tells tick-allergy (alpha-gal) patients which pill in their cabinet is safe, by NDC and lot, and compounds the ones that are not.
ideas.customer: Adults with alpha-gal syndrome, who pay cash for a membership and for compounded fills. CDC estimates up to 450,000 people were affected in 2010-2022, concentrated in the Southeast, Midwest and mid-Atlantic and spreading. A second wave of buyers is allergy clinics, health-system pharmacies and hospital perioperative teams, who would pay a license fee for the database.
ideas.problem: Drug makers are not required to disclose whether gelatin, glycerin, magnesium stearate or heparin came from a mammal. The label says 'gelatin' and nothing more. The free Alpha-gal Information (AGI) mammalian byproducts database works at ingredient level, not for the exact NDC and lot in the patient's hand. A pharmacist verifying one drug spends 30-90 minutes calling manufacturers. Then the wholesaler switches generic suppliers, the excipients change silently, and a patient who has been stable for a year ends up with anaphylaxis or a 2 a.m. ER visit. Patients and their Facebook groups crowd-source this by hand.
ideas.solution: 1) Build an NDC-level sourcing ledger. A pharmacist team sends templated requests to manufacturers for written excipient-source statements, and an LLM parses the replies and DailyMed SPL excipient lists. Each NDC gets a tier (plant or synthetic confirmed, mammal-derived, unknown) plus the date and lot range. 2) Sell a 'Safe Fill' membership that dispenses only verified NDCs, pins the manufacturer with a do-not-substitute request to the prescriber, and alerts the member when a source changes. 3) Compound unavailable items into HPMC vegetable capsules. This fits the 503A 'significant clinical difference' allowance because a documented allergy is a patient-specific reason, unlike copy compounding. 4) License the ledger to health systems and allergy groups.
ideas.why_now: Alpha-gal is now recognized as far more common than clinicians assumed, and the lone star tick's range keeps expanding. Regulators and payers have turned hostile to copy compounding after the 2025 GLP-1 shortage ended, so the legitimate lane is narrow, patient-specific allergy compounding, and this idea sits squarely in it. LLMs make parsing messy manufacturer letters and SPL data feasible for a two-person team, which was not true three years ago.
ideas.revenue_model: About $14 a month per patient membership (lookups, sourcing letters, source-change alerts, substitution management). Dispensing and compounding margin on cash-pay fills ($25-60 per compounded fill). B2B database license of $5k-25k a year per health system or allergy group. Optional paid sourcing-verification requests from hospitals for one-off drugs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not a list of bad ingredients. It is provenance per NDC and lot, which changes silently when a wholesaler swaps a generic supplier, and only the dispensing pharmacist sees the swap happen. Whoever holds a dated, manufacturer-confirmed ledger owns the trust of a patient group that currently does all of this by hand and pays cash for certainty.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick the 50 most-prescribed oral drugs plus anticoagulant alternatives. Send NDC-specific inquiry letters to manufacturers and publish a free 'verified so far' list to build search traffic and credibility. Join the alpha-gal patient communities and offer 100 founding members $9 a month for life. A pharmacist owner with a compounding license fills the first cash orders locally. Get a review letter from two allergists. File nonresident pharmacy license applications in the top tick-prevalence states, such as TN, KY, MO, VA, NC and AR.

ideas.title: Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers
ideas.one_liner: Independent pharmacies hold the half of the PBM ledger that employers never see, which is what the PBM actually paid the pharmacy. Pool it to run spread audits for self-insured employers, and give pharmacies a stay-or-leave calculator for their take-it-or-leave-it PBM contracts.
ideas.customer: Two sides. First, independent pharmacies, at $99-199 a month for benchmarking and a network-contract modeler. Second, self-funded local employers, school districts, counties and union funds (from 100 to 5,000 lives), plus the benefit consultants and TPAs that serve them, who pay per audit or a share of verified savings.
ideas.problem: The employer sees only what it paid the PBM. The PBM sees both sides and hides one. The pharmacy sees what it was paid and what it paid the wholesaler, but has no benchmark and no idea whether the network offer that arrives every Q4 for January 1 is worse than its peers' terms. Everyone negotiates blind. PBMs threaten a pharmacy with losing about a quarter of its business if it declines, and a plan sponsor cannot verify 'pass-through' claims.
ideas.solution: Read-only ingestion of the pharmacy's 835 remittance files and invoice costs from its pharmacy management system (PMS). Output 1) per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement benchmarked against NADAC and an anonymized peer pool. 2) A stay-or-leave model of each 2027 network offer built from the pharmacy's own claims mix. 3) With sponsor consent, a claim-level tie-out of the pharmacy-paid amounts against the employer's PBM claims file. That yields a true spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member, delivered as an audit the employer can use to renegotiate or move to a transparent PBM.
ideas.why_now: The contract season for January 2027 is happening right now, which gives a hard deadline and a free entry wedge. Employer fiduciaries are under pressure from ERISA suits over PBM costs, state PBM transparency laws and FTC scrutiny. Pharmacy closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores) have given local officials political will. OCR and LLM parsing of messy remit PDFs now makes onboarding a one-day job rather than a consulting project.
ideas.revenue_model: Pharmacy subscription of $99-199 a month, or free in exchange for data. Employer audit fees of about $8k-25k per mid-size sponsor, or 10-20% of first-year verified savings. Data licenses to state employee plans, attorneys general, employer coalitions and consultants at a higher tier.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Everyone in the PBM fight holds half a ledger, and only the pharmacy can prove the gap. Thirty pharmacies in one county reconstruct the local school district's and county government's spread at claim level. Independents will hand this data over willingly because it is the first ammunition they have ever had against take-it-or-leave-it contracts.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 15 pharmacies through the state independent pharmacy association with the pitch 'we will model your 2027 PBM offers free'. Build parsers for the three biggest PBMs' remit formats (the 835 EDI standard helps). Deliver the first stay-or-leave reports. Hire a healthcare attorney to structure data-use terms, since provider-manual confidentiality clauses and HIPAA de-identification are the main risk. Offer one local school district or county a free pilot spread audit and turn the result into a one-page case study.

ideas.title: Widow's First 90 Days, Sold Through Funeral Homes
ideas.one_liner: The pharmacy sees a death first, because refills stop. Package a pharmacist-led medicine cleanup and 90-day check-in program for the surviving spouse, and sell it to funeral homes as their aftercare offering.
ideas.customer: Independent funeral homes, which pay $95-195 per family or fold it into a package. Also out-of-town adult children, who pay $29-49 a month for someone local to watch over the surviving parent. Later, Medicare Advantage plans and PACE programs.
ideas.problem: When one spouse dies, the survivor often loses the person who managed the pillbox for both. The survivor skips or double-doses their own meds. The decedent's opioids and benzodiazepines sit in the house, where they can be diverted or swallowed by a grandchild. The first months after spousal loss carry a well-documented spike in illness and mortality, yet the funeral home hands over a grief booklet and the family scatters. No institution owns the medicine cabinet.
ideas.solution: A 'Steady' kit enrolled at the arrangement conference with one text. Within a week the pharmacist collects, counts and safely disposes of the decedent's meds, using the pharmacy's DEA-authorized collector status, which funeral homes lack. The pharmacist reconciles the survivor's own meds, resets med sync with adherence packaging and delivery, and flags deprescribing candidates for the doctor. Then come structured 30/60/90-day calls covering eating, sleeping, mood, falls and missed doses, with a report to the adult child and referrals to grief support or the physician when flags trip.
ideas.why_now: The first baby boomers turn 80 in 2026, so deaths in the 75-90 cohort will climb for two decades. Small funeral homes are squeezed by cremation and consolidators and need a differentiator beyond price. Independent pharmacies need new cash services as PBM margins collapse. Startups like Empathy have shown that families, employers and insurers pay for post-death help, but none touch medicines. Opioid-settlement money is funding take-back and safe disposal.
ideas.revenue_model: Funeral home pays per enrolled family, or the fee is folded into a package uplift. Families or adult children pay a subscription for the 90-day check-in service. The pharmacy earns on med sync, delivery and adherence packaging, plus MTM comprehensive medication review fees. Later, Medicare Advantage plans and PACE programs pay for bereavement-risk outreach.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A pharmacist learns of a death before the obituary runs, because the refill pattern stops and the survivor's profile changes. The pharmacist and the funeral director are the two professionals in every small town who deal with aging and dying. They have never shared a channel, and a disposal-authorized pharmacist is the only one who can legally take the leftover controlled drugs.
ideas.first_30_days: One pharmacy owner recruits two funeral homes in the same county. Build a one-page kit with a DEA-compliant collection procedure, a survivor med review checklist, a med-sync reset and a 30/60/90 call script. Pilot with 20 families, free to the funeral home at first, then $95 per family. Track bottles collected, discrepancies found and 90-day ER visits. Present the case study at the state funeral directors' association meeting and line up an MTM platform partner to bill the comprehensive medication reviews.

ideas.title: Rural Jail Pharmacy-in-a-Box for Independents
ideas.one_liner: Turn the local independent's blister packing, delivery and controlled-substance discipline into a per-inmate contract for the county jail that the sheriff is afraid of.
ideas.customer: Sheriffs, jail administrators and county commissions running jails of about 20-150 beds, whose risk pools and insurers care about medication liability. Independent pharmacies are a second customer, licensing the playbook and software.
ideas.problem: Jail medication is a sheriff's biggest lawsuit exposure: missed doses, withdrawal, wrong-inmate errors, controlled-substance counts. Small jails run it with a deputy, a clipboard and a nurse who visits two days a week. Mail-order jail pharmacies take 3-5 days, so first-night meds come from the ER or a deputy's personal trip to the drugstore. Buprenorphine and other opioid-treatment mandates funded by opioid settlements add complexity. Meanwhile local independents already run the identical workflow for nursing homes.
ideas.solution: A repeatable program with same-day intake verification (call the outside pharmacy, check the PDMP). Barcode blister-packed med pass with an offline-capable eMAR on a tablet. Controlled-substance counts with dual sign-off and photo audit. An emergency kit and a monthly consultant-pharmacist review. A 30-day bridge supply at release. Sold as a playbook, software and group-purchasing bundle so any independent can become the county's jail pharmacy, with master agreements through state association-of-counties risk pools.
ideas.why_now: Wellpath's late-2024 bankruptcy and the contract turnover that followed left counties scrambling for medical vendors. Deaths-in-custody litigation keeps rising. Opioid-settlement dollars are flowing to county jails for medication for opioid use disorder. A growing number of state Medicaid reentry waivers require medication continuity at release. Independents need any revenue line that does not depend on PBM reimbursement.
ideas.revenue_model: County per-diem or monthly retainer (roughly $1,500-6,000 a month per small jail, to be validated by state). The pharmacy pays a 10-15% platform fee plus $300-600 a month for the software. Additional revenue from risk-pool partnership programs and discharge-supply services.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Rural jail medication is not a healthcare problem, it is a liability problem the sheriff cannot outsource to a national vendor that ships in five days. The real buyer is the county risk pool and insurer, and the independent pharmacist next door is the only entity that can deliver in thirty minutes. Small contracts often fall below county bid thresholds, and the sheriff already knows the pharmacist by first name.
ideas.first_30_days: The pharmacist calls the sheriff in their own county and offers a 60-day pilot at cost. Audit the jail's med room and write a one-page deficiency list. Propose eMAR plus packaging. Check the state pharmacy board's rules for institutional or correctional pharmacy licensure. Pitch the results to the state sheriffs' association and the county risk pool, and recruit two neighboring independents to copy the model.

ideas.title: Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds
ideas.one_liner: Fund the 3-4 week float independent pharmacies now carry on Medicare's negotiated-price drugs, underwritten on predictable refund data, before Ozempic joins the list in January.
ideas.customer: Independent pharmacies with senior-heavy books, especially those serving long-term care, then 5-50 store groups and PSAOs. Average exposure is estimated at over $27,000 a month per community pharmacy.
ideas.problem: Since January 1, 2026, pharmacies pay wholesalers full price for Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Farxiga, Januvia, Entresto and others, dispense at Medicare's Maximum Fair Price, and wait weeks for the difference to arrive through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator. Estimates put the float at $27k+ a month for the average community pharmacy, over $500M a month industry-wide, on top of wholesalers who still auto-debit weekly. On thin margins that is a real solvency risk. Banks see a pharmacy, not an insured refund.
ideas.solution: Start with a reconciliation tool that ingests the pharmacy's PMS claims export and the MTF remittance files and shows late or missing refunds. Then offer a non-recourse advance of about 90% of the expected refund on each week's MFP claims, repaid from the actual MTF payment through a controlled deposit account or sweep. Confirm with CMS and the facilitator what payment-routing options exist, and fall back to a bank-account sweep if third-party routing is not allowed.
ideas.why_now: The program only became real on January 1, 2026, and it is already causing cash-flow warnings from pharmacy coalitions. On January 1, 2027, 15 more drugs join, including semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus), which multiplies the float. Wholesalers have not yet solved it and the bank market does not understand it, so there is a window of a few quarters before someone standardizes the answer.
ideas.revenue_model: A fee of about 1-1.75% per advance cycle, which works out to roughly 15-25% annualized, plus a $99 a month reconciliation subscription. Contingency of about 10% on missing refunds recovered. Later, sell or syndicate the receivables to a credit fund.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: To a bank this looks like distress lending to a struggling small business. In reality it is close to prime paper: the obligor is a drug manufacturer with a statutory duty to pay, routed through a federal facilitator, backed by claim-level data. Only someone who knows how PMS claims map to MFP eligibility, and how a reversal or dispute can claw a refund back, can underwrite it. The free reconciliation report is the wedge that gets the data before any money goes out.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer a free 'find my missing refunds' report to 25 pharmacies through state association newsletters and pharmacy owner Facebook groups. Line up a $500k credit line from a regional bank or family office and keep the first ten advances small. Talk to a fintech attorney about commercial-financing disclosure laws by state. Approach one PSAO about distribution.

ideas.title: Rain-Day Revenue Insurance for Patio Restaurants
ideas.one_liner: Parametric weather cover for restaurants: pick your bad-weather trigger, get paid automatically when it hits, with payouts calibrated to your own POS history.
ideas.customer: Independent restaurants and bars with 1-10 units and meaningful patio or walk-up dependence, starting in weather-volatile metros (rain, extreme heat, wildfire smoke). The owner pays a seasonal premium of roughly $40-150 per location per month. A licensed MGA/carrier partner and reinsurer sit behind the product.
ideas.problem: A rainy Friday, a 105F heat-index evening or a smoke day (AQI over 150) can cut a patio-dependent night by 30-50%. The food is already prepped and the staff are already scheduled, so almost all of the lost revenue is lost margin. Business-interruption insurance needs physical damage, so weather-driven demand loss is uninsured. Every owner knows their 'rain tax' (I know a wet Saturday costs me several thousand dollars), yet no one sells a hedge for it.
ideas.solution: Owners connect Toast, Square or Clover, and we ingest 12-24 months of hourly sales. We fit each location's loss curve against local weather-station history, for example rain over 0.15 in between 5 and 9pm Fri-Sun, or heat index above 105. The owner picks triggers and a fixed payout per trigger day. When the station data crosses the threshold, the payout goes out automatically by instant rails, with no claim and no adjuster. Because triggers are calibrated per restaurant, basis risk is low, which is what has kept carriers away from this segment. We sell it as a seasonal policy with a monthly premium.
ideas.why_now: POS APIs now give clean hourly sales for thousands of independents in minutes. Weather-station and air-quality data are cheap and auditable. Instant payment rails (FedNow, RTP) exist. Heat domes and smoke seasons are making weather volatility a top-3 owner complaint. Reinsurers are hungry for parametric programs, and restaurants face rising conventional premiums that push them to look for smarter cover. I could not re-verify current competitors this session, so check the existing parametric MGAs and event-cancellation carriers before building.
ideas.revenue_model: MGA commission plus underwriting margin on premium, typically 15-30% of premium retained as fee and MGA share. Roughly $500-1,800 per location per year in premium. Add a fee for the POS-calibrated loss-curve analytics, sold to carriers and reinsurers as a data product.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The trick is that the owner's POS data, not a claims adjuster, is the underwriting. Basis risk is what kills parametric for small businesses, and a restaurant's own hourly sales history fixes it. Insurers think restaurants are too heterogeneous to price. They are only heterogeneous until you fit each one separately. The loss is also asymmetric: prepped food and committed labor mean a payout only has to cover the lost contribution margin, not the revenue, so premiums can be low.
ideas.first_30_days: Use my two locations' POS exports plus 10 friendly patio owners' data to fit loss curves and prove the weather-to-sales correlation. Publish a free 'Rain Tax Report' for one metro to generate leads. Sign a licensed MGA or fronting-carrier partner. Collect 10-15 signed letters of intent at about $60 per month for the next patio season. Since it is late September, use the off-season to finish modeling and pre-sell spring renewals.

ideas.title: Fry-Oil Co-op Escaping Evergreen Renderer Contracts
ideas.one_liner: Aggregate independent restaurants' used cooking oil, sell it to biofuel buyers at market with sensor-verified traceability, and hand the owner the check the big renderer keeps.
ideas.customer: Independent restaurants and small chains with 2-20 fryer-heavy units are the supply side and pay no fee. Local independent oil collectors, biodiesel, renewable diesel and SAF feedstock processors and brokers are the demand side and pay the co-op. Revenue is the spread plus a small sensor rental fee.
ideas.problem: Used fry oil is a commodity that biofuel makers have been bidding up, yet independents are locked into 3-year auto-renewing pickup contracts with a large renderer or bin company. The restaurant is paid a pittance or nothing, or is even charged fees. Bins overflow, which brings health-code and odor problems. Thieves steal oil at night, and nobody reconciles what the oil is actually worth. Owners don't switch because the termination window is a 60-90 day certified-letter deadline buried in the contract, and nobody has time to run a bid.
ideas.solution: A co-op platform that: (1) tracks each member's contract renewal date and files the non-renewal notice on time; (2) runs a monthly reverse auction among local collectors so that volume, not the restaurant, gets the price; (3) installs a roughly $40 ultrasonic fill sensor and a lockable tank cap, so pickups trigger at 80% full and every pickup is photo- or QR-verified; (4) issues a statement per pickup indexed to a published used-cooking-oil price series; and (5) produces per-restaurant chain-of-custody records that renewable-fuel producers need to prove domestic, traceable feedstock.
ideas.why_now: As I understand it, federal clean-fuel incentives (45Z) now favor North American feedstock, and concern about mislabeled imported used oil has raised the value of traceable domestic oil. Renewable diesel and SAF capacity keeps growing. Cheap cellular fill sensors are widely available. Restaurants' margins are so thin that any found cash gets attention. Verify the current feedstock price index and the 45Z sourcing rules before you pitch.
ideas.revenue_model: 20-30% spread on oil sold, indexed and transparent, plus $10-30 per month for the sensor and tank lock. Later add a premium for verified-traceable oil sold to fuel producers, and carbon-intensity documentation fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The incumbent's real product is the locked contract and route density, not the oil service, so the way in is the calendar rather than a better price. The contract renewal date is the CRM key: a 90-day-out certified non-renewal letter, filed for the owner, is the growth engine. Owners think they are getting 'free removal', so nobody shops it. Also, per-restaurant traceability is worth more to fuel buyers than the oil's volume alone.
ideas.first_30_days: Walk one restaurant row and photograph each bin's contract label, and note the pickup company and renewal date for 40 restaurants in one metro. Sign one local collector or small biodiesel maker as a buyer with a written price index. Enroll 8-10 off-contract or month-to-month members, including my own two locations. Install sensors and lock caps, run the first monthly auction, and show each owner a side-by-side statement of what their old vendor paid versus what the co-op did.

ideas.title: Restaurant Kitchens as Chefs for Small Care Homes
ideas.one_liner: License a turnkey program that lets restaurants use dead hours to cook dietitian-approved, texture-modified meals for 6-20 bed assisted-living and adult-family homes that big foodservice ignores.
ideas.customer: Operators of small licensed residential care homes (adult family homes, board-and-care, personal care homes, small RCFEs) pay per resident per day, typically $8-12 for lunch and dinner. Adult children pay for premium 'chef-cooked' upgrades. The restaurant is the supplier, and the platform takes a license fee and revenue share.
ideas.problem: In a small care home, food is the main daily pleasure and the top resident complaint, yet it is cooked by overworked caregivers from warehouse-club and broadline food, with little variety and hard-to-manage special diets (mechanical soft, pureed, low-sodium, diabetic). Sodexo and Compass do not serve 6-bed homes and meals-on-wheels serves people at home. Meanwhile my kitchens sit idle from 2 to 5pm and on slow days, my cooks want more hours, and my dine-in traffic is soft.
ideas.solution: A meal program in a box for restaurants: a rotating 5-week menu library with dietitian sign-off and texture-modified variants (IDDSI levels), allergen and diet labels, batch-cook and cook-chill (or same-day hot delivery) SOPs, a state-specific health-department pre-clearance checklist and HACCP plan templates, routing and billing software, and a contracted registered dietitian on retainer. The restaurant cooks in dead hours and delivers 2-3 times a week in labeled pans, and the care home reheats. Ten homes at about $17-22k per year each is $170-220k of found revenue at healthy contribution margin on capacity that was previously idle.
ideas.why_now: The 65+ population is growing fast (the 'Peak 65' wave runs through about 2027). Families are shifting to small, cheaper residential homes rather than large assisted-living campuses. Restaurant dine-in traffic has been soft and owners are actively looking for non-traffic revenue. Kitchen labor is short, and steady off-peak hours help retention. Public state license lists make the small-home buyer easy to find. I couldn't verify current home counts this session, so pull the licensing-list counts state by state before building.
ideas.revenue_model: Onboarding fee of $1-2k per restaurant, plus 10-15% of meal revenue, plus software billing at about $100 per month per restaurant. Optional premium tier for adult-child paid 'chef upgrades' and dietitian services.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The gold is in the mismatch between an idle asset and an ignored customer. Small-home operators are often immigrant nurses and caregivers running a tiny business with no procurement power, and no large foodservice company will serve them, but a two-location restaurant can absorb a 300-meal-per-week route into dead hours at nearly zero marginal labor cost. What a restaurant cannot do alone is the compliance layer (texture modification, diet labeling, dietitian review, regulator pre-clearance), and that is the product.
ideas.first_30_days: Pull the state's public list of small residential care homes and shortlist 30 within a 15-minute drive. Call my health department to confirm what is required to supply prepared meals from a licensed restaurant to a licensed facility. Hire a freelance registered dietitian by the hour for one 2-week menu. Offer 3 homes a free trial week, then convert them at about $9 per resident per day. Document the SOPs and the regulator's answer as the first version of the product.

ideas.title: Menu Trial Lab: Restaurants as Food-Brand Test Sites
ideas.one_liner: A network of two-to-five-unit restaurants that run randomized menu experiments for food brands and commodity boards, and get paid for it.
ideas.customer: Emerging food and beverage brands (sauces, blended or alternative proteins, beverages), commodity checkoff boards (beef, pork, dairy, potato, avocado and similar), and distributor private-label teams pay $10-25k per trial. Independent operators are paid a fee and free product and get menu-engineering results back.
ideas.problem: Foodservice launches fail because the operator's ROI is unproven, not because guests dislike the item. Line speed, storage, training, plate cost and cannibalization decide whether an item survives. Brands pay for sales reps, menu-placement deals and consumer surveys, but survey data measures stated preference. The item then sits in my walk-in. Reps tell operators 'it sells' with no data to prove it.
ideas.solution: Recruit a network of 2-5-unit independents who connect Toast, Square or Clover. Each trial is a randomized matched-pair test: the item is on the menu at one location and not at its twin, then swapped, and we run a difference-in-differences on attach rate, check average, cannibalization, plate cost and contribution margin per cover. The deliverable is a 'Menu Adoption Scorecard' plus an operator-facing ROI one-pager the brand's reps and distributors can use to close accounts. Automated matched-pair design and automated POS reading keep unit costs low.
ideas.why_now: Beef, coffee, cocoa and dairy cost pressure has kept operators reformulating (blends, substitutions) since 2025, and brands need proof under tighter budgets. POS platform APIs and partner ecosystems now make continuous read access practical at scale. AI makes experiment design and reporting cheap. Commodity boards and distributors are under pressure to show operator-level ROI. I could not verify whether an existing network already sells this, so check Datassential, Technomic and distributor pilot programs first.
ideas.revenue_model: Fee per trial ($10-25k) paid by the brand or board, with a portion (say $500-2,000) paid to each participating operator. Later, annual data subscriptions for brand teams and 'scorecard' licensing to distributors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A two-location owner is a natural experimenter, since it is the only cheap way to run a true A/B with identical kitchens, menus and staff. Nobody in food innovation uses that. The buyer's real question is 'will an operator make money and keep it on the menu', which no consumer panel answers. The moat is the operator network and their POS data, not the analytics.
ideas.first_30_days: Post in owner Facebook groups and a regional restaurant association to recruit 10 two-to-five-unit operators, including my own two locations as pilot sites. Approach 5 emerging brands at a regional foodservice show with a $5-8k, four-week matched-pair trial. Run my first trial in my own two restaurants and turn the results into a 3-page scorecard to use as the sales collateral for the next brand.

ideas.title: Predict Walk-In Cooler Failures Via Refrigeration Techs
ideas.one_liner: White-label predictive monitoring that local commercial-refrigeration companies sell as a maintenance plan, so a failing compressor becomes a Tuesday service visit rather than a Saturday-night emergency.
ideas.customer: Independent commercial refrigeration and HVAC-R service companies with 5-50 techs, who pay roughly $8-12 per monitored compressor per month and resell at $25-40 inside a maintenance plan. The restaurant is the end payer. A later add-on is a spoilage-insurer premium discount.
ideas.problem: A walk-in dies on Saturday at 9pm. That means an emergency call at 2-3x the rate and $8-15k of protein and dairy in the dumpster, sometimes a closed kitchen. Temperature-probe alerts only fire after the box is already warm, so they are too late. The real early signals are in the power draw: rising duty cycle from dirty condenser coils, failing fan motors and capacitors, low charge, short-cycling, and defrost heater faults. Techs spend their weekends on emergencies and have almost no recurring revenue.
ideas.solution: Clip-on current-sensing hardware (roughly $25-40 bill of materials) with a cellular or Wi-Fi gateway on each compressor and condenser fan. A model compares duty cycle and amp draw against ambient kitchen temperature and defrost cycles to flag drift weeks before the box warms. It creates a scheduled work order in the contractor's dispatch system (for example ServiceTitan) with the likely fault and parts to bring. The contractor sells it as a 'Sunday-proof plan' and gets the white-label dashboard and monthly reports.
ideas.why_now: Cellular IoT and current sensors are very cheap. Field-service software has spread through small trades, so integrations are possible. Skilled refrigeration techs are scarce and contractors need each tech to cover more boxes. The HFC phasedown (AIM Act) is changing refrigerants and service complexity, pushing repair-versus-replace decisions. Power prices are climbing, so efficiency drift now costs owners visibly.
ideas.revenue_model: Recurring B2B2B: $8-12 per monitored compressor per month to the contractor, plus hardware at cost and a per-contractor platform fee. Later, add insurer partnerships that pay for verified spoilage-loss reductions.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The real distribution channel for restaurant equipment tech is not SaaS marketing to owners. It is 'my guy': the one refrigeration tech who answers his phone. Owners trust him, he holds the keys and the relationship, and he hates 2am calls and lacks recurring revenue. Sell to Mike, not to me. The signal is also cheaper than probes: amp draw predicts failures that temperature only reveals when it is too late.
ideas.first_30_days: Instrument 10-15 compressors and condenser fans across my two locations and five friends' restaurants with off-the-shelf clamp sensors. Log data and record every failure. Sign 2-3 local refrigeration companies as design partners with a free 60-day pilot of 50 sensors. Use the first 'caught it before Saturday' event as the case study, then sell the plan to that contractor's other accounts.

ideas.title: Pay Home Inspectors to Find Lead Pipes
ideas.one_liner: A micro-bounty network that pays home inspectors, plumbers and water-heater installers to photograph where the service line enters the basement, with AI classification, so utilities can clear 'unknown material' lines for about $40 each instead of $500-3,000 each.
ideas.customer: Mid-size municipal and district water utilities (20k-300k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their published lead service line inventory. The buyer is the utility director or the lead program manager. A secondary payer is the home buyer, who pays about $29 for a 'Lead Line Certificate' add-on at inspection.
ideas.problem: Since the lead and copper inventory requirement, every system has had to classify each service line as lead, galvanized-requiring-replacement, non-lead or unknown. Unknowns are a legal and financial liability, and they are hard to shrink. The only sure verification is potholing or excavation, which costs hundreds to thousands of dollars per line. Customer self-ID by mailer gets a response rate of roughly 10-25%. Absentee landlords and LLCs almost never answer. Utility crews can't look inside private basements, so tens of thousands of unknowns sit in the spreadsheet for years.
ideas.solution: A mobile app with a fixed 3-photo protocol: the pipe where it enters the building, a scratch or magnet test close-up, and the meter serial number with the address. A vision model classifies the pipe as copper, galvanized, lead, PEX, PVC or HDPE, or flags it as unresolved. Humans QA the low-confidence cases. Each submission is geo-verified and tamper-evident, and exports in the format the state inventory portal expects. Inspectors and plumbers earn $15-25 per verified line, and the platform earns the spread. The utility gets a reconciled inventory feed and a dashboard showing unknowns falling by ZIP code. The consumer add-on (inspector-branded certificate, sold to the buyer) pays the inspector while giving the utility free data.
ideas.why_now: The first inventories were filed in late 2024, and public analyses showed millions of lines still classified 'unknown'. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements set a 10-year replacement clock that starts around 2027, though federal details keep being revisited and litigated. Several states have their own replacement statutes that don't depend on the federal rule. The $15B in dedicated infrastructure-law lead line money is moving through state revolving funds under spend-down pressure. Vision models are only now accurate enough to classify pipe photos. (Regulatory details are from memory. Verify state acceptance rules before pitching.)
ideas.revenue_model: Utilities pay $30-60 per verified line, sold as a per-line contract that fits under small-purchase thresholds. A $10-25k pilot is typical, followed by annual contracts. The consumer-paid certificate ($29) is split with the inspector. Later products are inventory-reconciliation SaaS and an access-agreement workflow for replacement crews.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Utilities think they have a data problem, but they have an eyeballs-in-basements problem. Every home sale (an inspector visits) and every water heater swap (a plumber stands three feet from the service entry) already puts a paid expert next to the exact pipe that matters. Nobody has paid them for a photo yet. Excavation is the wrong tool for a question that visual inspection answers for almost nothing.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one state that accepts documented visual or contractor verification. Pick two utilities in it whose public inventories are more than 40% unknown. Recruit 30 inspectors through local InterNACHI and ASHI chapter meetups and Facebook groups, and pay a launch bonus per photo set. Run a 200-line pilot. Have the utility pothole 30 of those lines as ground truth, then publish the accuracy numbers. Close a $15-25k pilot purchase order with the first utility, using the small-purchase limit that many cities set at $25-50k so no council vote is needed.

ideas.title: Instant Will-Serve Letters From Hydraulic Models
ideas.one_liner: Turn a utility's calibrated hydraulic model into a self-serve 'can you serve this address?' oracle that issues fire-flow and will-serve determinations in 48 hours instead of 4 weeks. It starts with developers and sprinkler designers and grows into a water-readiness index for data center and fab site selectors.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size water utilities and the consulting engineering firms that maintain their models are the sellers. The payers are housing developers and fire sprinkler design firms ($250-2,000 per request), then data center, fab and beverage-plant site selection teams ($20-100k per year for the readiness data).
ideas.problem: Every subdivision, sprinkler design and industrial hookup needs a will-serve or fire-flow letter. Utilities own a calibrated hydraulic model (WaterGEMS, InfoWater, EPANET), but one or two engineers, or an outside consultant billing $2-8k per run, can operate it. Requests queue for weeks and stall housing and economic development. Worse, the answer 'we have plenty of water' is meaningless. The binding limits are max-day and peak-hour pressure in one pressure zone, fire reserve storage, tank turnover and water age, and the wastewater plant's discharge limits. Big buyers don't know that, and many utilities can't answer within the time a site-selection process allows.
ideas.solution: Ingest the utility's model file (.inp or vendor formats) and pre-compute a grid of scenarios. For each node and pressure zone, calculate available fire flow at a 20 psi residual, the maximum added demand before minimum-pressure or velocity limits break, and the effect on tank cycling and water age. Wrap it in a web form and API: enter address, demand, fire-flow requirement, and get a preliminary letter with the utility's letterhead, assumptions and limits. Exceptions go to the utility's licensed engineer for review and stamp. Utilities set the fee and keep most of it. The large-load layer adds wastewater and pretreatment limits, reclaimed-water availability, drought stage and water-rights status. It is published as a 'water hookup readiness' score by utility, like the power-availability maps that data center developers already buy.
ideas.why_now: The data center build-out has made water availability a headline and a local permitting fight, and site selection teams already buy power-availability intelligence but have no water equivalent. Housing permitting reform is speeding the approvals that come before utility review, which makes the utility review the bottleneck. Open-source tooling (EPANET and Sandia's WNTR) plus LLM agents that can read model files and draft letters make productizing this feasible for a small team. Many utilities finished models under recent risk-and-resilience assessments and master plans, so the models exist and are unused.
ideas.revenue_model: Utility SaaS of $15-40k per year, or free in exchange for a revenue share on developer fees. Per-request fees of $250-2,000 paid by developers, with the utility keeping 50-70%. Data subscriptions of $20-100k per year to site selectors, land brokers and hyperscaler real-estate teams. A consulting-firm channel where the engineering firm resells to its 10-30 utility clients.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not water. It is the one person who is allowed to run the model. The calibrated model is the most valuable unused asset a utility owns, and the answer developers want is hydraulic (peak-day and fire-flow at one node), not a volume in an annual water permit.
ideas.first_30_days: Approach one consulting engineering firm that maintains models for 10 or more small utilities and pitch productizing its most repeated task. Build a thin front end on WNTR or EPANET and offer one utility a free pilot: a public fire-flow map plus a letter template. Run the first 20 requests semi-manually, with the engineer generating and signing outputs in the background. Charge local sprinkler design firms $250 per fire-flow letter. Use the results to show turnaround times to two more utilities and to start a data-center-readiness prototype for one region.

ideas.title: Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue
ideas.one_liner: Find the 'ghost parcels' and slow big meters that leak revenue out of a utility, using assessor rolls, building footprints, imagery and billing data, and get paid 20-30% of what is recovered so the city risks nothing.
ideas.customer: City, county and district water and sewer utilities with 10k-200k connections. The buyer is the finance director or utility director who is facing a council fight over the next rate increase.
ideas.problem: Utilities are raising rates 5-10% a year to fund PFAS treatment, lead line replacement and aging pipes, and councils are pushing back on affordability. Meanwhile revenue leaks out in places nobody owns: structures with no water account (unpermitted ADUs on shared meters, converted garages, fire and irrigation taps never billed), commercial compound meters that are 20-30 years old and under-register at low flows, meters swapped without the account being updated, stopped or zero-read accounts that never get investigated, and sewer-only accounts billed off a bad water read. The customer information system, the GIS parcel layer and the assessor roll sit in different departments. Nobody owns the join, and nobody has staff to do it.
ideas.solution: Join the utility's account list and consumption history to the assessor roll (building sq ft, units, use code), permits, open building-footprint datasets and aerial imagery (pools, irrigated area, added structures). Build an expected-consumption model by parcel. Rank the mismatches: no account at all, consumption far below expected, sudden step-downs after a meter change, and large meters whose low-flow profile looks wrong. A small field crew and a meter-test partner verify the top leads. The utility gets a documented recovery list with legal-ready evidence, back-billing calculations that respect the state's limits, and a meter-replacement plan. The firm takes 20-30% of first-year recovered incremental revenue.
ideas.why_now: Rate shock and affordability politics in 2025-26 make 'recover what we're owed before raising rates' an easy story for council. Open building-footprint datasets and cheap vision AI make expected-consumption modeling accessible to a two-person team, and utilities that finished smart-meter rollouts now have interval data that has never been analyzed for revenue. Contingency work also clears procurement easily because there is no upfront cost.
ideas.revenue_model: Contingency of 20-30% on the first 12-24 months of recovered annualized revenue, plus a fixed fee for a meter-testing and replacement plan. Later, a recurring SaaS monitor ($1-3 per 100 accounts per month). Optional referral fees from meter and test vendors.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The leak that matters is not in the pipe. Large commercial meters are about 10-20% of accounts but 40-60% of revenue, and the oldest ones quietly under-register the low flows that hospitals, hotels and factories use all night. The utility never sees this loss because the meter is the thing measuring it.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick a county whose assessor roll and building footprints are downloadable and whose utility publishes or will release account addresses (public-records request). Run a free scan and generate 20 named addresses with expected versus billed usage. Cold-email finance directors at five utilities with 'we'll show you 20 unbilled addresses before you sign anything'. Sign the first contingency contract with a city that has a rate hearing scheduled, and verify leads with a hired meter-testing subcontractor.

ideas.title: Water Towers as Virtual Power Plants
ideas.one_liner: Aggregate municipal pump stations and elevated tanks into a controllable flexible load that dodges peak-coincident charges and earns demand-response and capacity payments, with a hard guarantee on pressure and fire reserve and an operator veto.
ideas.customer: Cities and districts that pump water, especially cities that own both the electric and water departments (common in the Midwest, Texas and the Southeast) and utilities with transmission-level or large demand-charge accounts. The buyer is the utilities director or the city manager, with the finance director as the champion.
ideas.problem: Electricity is one of the largest controllable costs for a pumped water system. Yet most pumping schedules are simple level setpoints written years ago, and operators keep tanks fat out of habit and fear. The unspoken rule is that nobody ever got fired for a full tank. Meanwhile the grid has turned pumping hours into money. Peak-coincident charges such as 4CP in ERCOT and peak load contribution tags in PJM are set by just a handful of hours per year. Capacity prices have spiked in recent auctions. Big load additions are pushing retail rates up. Water utilities are physically able to shift a large share of pumping, but no vendor is selling it to the 10-100k-population systems in a form an operator trusts.
ideas.solution: A small edge box or cloud service that reads tank levels, pump status and pressure from SCADA (OPC-UA or Modbus, read-only at first). It computes safe curtailment windows per station with hard constraints: fire and emergency reserve never touched, minimum pressure kept, projected demand over the event covered, water-age limits respected. It pre-cools tanks before predicted grid peaks and auto-releases if any constraint is threatened. Operators see one screen and can veto or end an event in one tap. Phase one is pure peak-coincident avoidance and time-of-use shifting, which needs no market enrollment. Phase two enrolls the stations as a curtailment resource through a demand-response aggregator partner or directly.
ideas.why_now: Recent PJM capacity auctions cleared at or near the price cap, on the order of $100k or more per curtailable megawatt per year before an aggregator's cut. Data center load growth is pushing capacity and transmission costs into retail rates, and RTOs and utilities are expanding demand-response programs. Edge controllers and OPC-UA gateways are cheap, and small teams can now build reliable forecasting for tank levels and peak intervals. (Auction figures are from memory. Verify current prices before pitching.)
ideas.revenue_model: 25-40% of verified savings and demand-response revenue, with no upfront cost to the utility and a small monthly platform fee. Utilities with both electric and water departments can be sold a bundled controls contract.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The constraint is not physical but psychological and legal: operators are (rightly) terrified of a pressure or fire-flow failure. The winning product is not optimization software but a guarantee with a veto. Sell the operator the ability to stop it at any moment and the CFO the savings. Also, water and electric are often the same city, and the city has never put both budgets on one page.
ideas.first_30_days: Target three small cities that own both electric and water in ERCOT or PJM territory and have published tariffs. Get read-only SCADA access at one pump station, or historical CSV exports of tank levels and pump runs. Replay a year of the data to show what a 4CP or PLC avoidance schedule would have saved with reserves untouched. Bring that dollar figure to the city manager, and sign a shared-savings pilot on one pump station.

ideas.title: Passive Wellness Alerts From Water Meter Patterns
ideas.one_liner: A subscription that texts an adult child, or their parent's home-care agency, when an older person living alone has no expected water activity: no wearable, no camera, just the meter that is already on the house.
ideas.customer: Adult children of seniors who live alone ($12-19 per month). Home-care agencies and Area Agencies on Aging, which pay about $15-25 per client per month for a passive check on clients between visits. Later, Medicare Advantage plans offering supplemental benefits, at a per-member-per-month rate. Utilities are the channel partner, not the main payer.
ideas.problem: Roughly a quarter or more of Americans aged 65 and older live alone. Existing safety products get abandoned: pendants are left on the nightstand, wearables aren't charged, and cameras feel like surveillance and get unplugged. Families end up making anxious phone calls. Meanwhile the utility already has hour-level (or finer) consumption data from its smart meter, used only for bill disputes and leak alerts. Nobody has to wear or charge a meter.
ideas.solution: Learn each household's rhythm from interval water data: first use in the morning, number of daily events, typical overnight quiet. Alert on: no water event by the person's usual time plus a buffer, unusually long or repeated overnight use (possible wandering or confusion), continuous flow (leak or overflow), and sudden spikes. Escalate by text to a family member, then to a designated neighbor or a non-emergency wellness-check partner. Two data paths. Path A is a $40-bill-of-materials clamp-on or pulse reader on the customer's own meter, installed in 15 minutes by a caregiver, which needs no utility integration. Path B is a customer-consented feed from the utility's smart-meter system, with no hardware and utility co-branding. Leak protection is a free bonus that sells the same product to the utility.
ideas.why_now: The oldest baby boomers are now in their 80s, and 'Peak 65' has meant around 4 million Americans turning 65 every year through 2027. Home-care labor is scarce, so agencies need passive tools that extend a caregiver's reach. Smart-meter adoption among mid-size and large water utilities is now high, and those utilities are looking for customer-engagement wins after the billing complaints that followed rollouts. Green Button-style customer-directed data sharing exists for electricity but is almost absent for water. LLMs can also explain a pattern change in plain language to worried families.
ideas.revenue_model: Family subscription of $12-19 per month, plus optional hardware at cost or $49. B2B2C contracts with home-care agencies at $15-25 per client per month. Revenue share or flat fees from utilities per opted-in household. Later, Medicare Advantage supplemental-benefit contracts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Water use is the most honest sign of life in a house. Nobody can skip flushing for 36 hours, and it can't be faked, forgotten or unplugged. Japan's Zojirushi 'mimamori' kettle proved families will pay for a signal from an ordinary appliance. A utility meter is the same idea at the level of the whole house, and utilities are sitting on the data with no product.
ideas.first_30_days: Partner with two or three local home-care agencies and an Area Agency on Aging. Recruit 30 consenting seniors or families through caregiver support groups and Facebook groups for adult children. Install pulse or clamp-on readers on meters that support them, and run a 30-day baseline. Alert families by text and measure false-alarm and helpfulness rates. In parallel, approach one mid-size smart-meter utility with an opt-in pilot: consented data sharing at no cost, with the utility's logo on the program. Charge families $15 per month from day 31.

ideas.title: Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties
ideas.one_liner: A success-fee auditor that finds repaired aircraft components that failed inside the shop's warranty window, and turns them into filed claims and cash.
ideas.customer: Small and mid-size operators with their own stores and a thin materials team. That means regional airlines, Part 135 cargo feeders and air-ambulance fleets, and Part 145 shops that buy their own exchange units. They pay 20-25% of whatever cash or credit is recovered, and nothing up front.
ideas.problem: A repaired starter-generator, bleed valve, hydraulic pump or fuel control that fails 4 months after the shop visit is often covered by warranty. Almost nobody claims it. The tech pulling the unit at 3 AM is trying to make a 6 AM departure and never sees the warranty terms. The repair invoice sits in accounts payable as a PDF. The removal record sits in the maintenance system, and hours and cycles sit in a third place. One materials coordinator owns thousands of removals a year, with 30-90 day claim windows. Three other leaks go unclaimed as well: 'no fault found' evaluation fees on units that were still under warranty, unreturned exchange cores that turn into penalty charges, and repair turnaround-time guarantees that shops never credit because nobody compares PO date to receipt date.
ideas.solution: Ingest three exports: removals and installs, PO and repair invoices (PDFs read with an LLM extractor), and the negotiated warranty terms. Match by part number and serial number, including interchangeable P/Ns. Flag every in-warranty failure, late repair turn, disputable NFF fee and open core. Then draft the claim on each vendor's own template, track it to a paid credit, and re-run monthly. Add a 3 AM 'is this unit under warranty?' lookup for maintenance control, so the claim gets started at the moment of removal.
ideas.why_now: Airline cost pressure on regionals is high, and mechanic wages rose sharply in 2024-2026, so labor cost per removal is up. Materials teams are being cut while fleets stay old. LLM invoice and PDF extraction only became reliable and cheap enough in the last 18 months, and that is the missing link, because the money sits in unstructured AP documents that MRO software never reads.
ideas.revenue_model: Contingency fee of 20-25% of recovered cash and credits, with a 12-month tail on the audit. Later add a $2-5k per month SaaS tier for continuous monitoring, and sell benchmark data on shop warranty behavior to airline procurement teams.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The leak is not in the maintenance system, it is in accounts payable. The tech who removes the part, the coordinator who could file the claim and the department that paid the invoice never share a screen. MRO software vendors will not fix it because warranty terms live in negotiated PDFs, not fields. Repair shops know most eligible claims are never filed, and they price that into their rates. A contingency auditor is the same playbook as freight-audit and telecom-audit firms, aimed at a niche nobody has covered.
ideas.first_30_days: Pitch 10 directors of maintenance and materials managers at small regionals, cargo feeders and helicopter EMS operators. Offer a free 12-month leakage audit, and ask them for the three exports. Build the matcher in Python plus an LLM invoice parser, and use a retired warranty or materials coordinator as a paid advisor for vendor quirks. Deliver a ranked claim list to the first 2-3 customers, file the claims yourself, and sign the success-fee agreement on the first credit memo. Publish the aggregate audit finding, such as the percentage of eligible failures that were never claimed, as the lead magnet.

ideas.title: Certified Scrap Kill for Aircraft Parts
ideas.one_liner: A mobile crew and app that destroys, photographs and certifies scrapped aircraft parts so they can never resurface as fake 'serviceable' parts, and sells the segregated metal.
ideas.customer: Regional airline stores and quality departments, Part 145 repair stations, lessors managing teardowns and part-outs, and engine and component shops. They pay a per-event fee, partly offset by a share of the alloy value.
ideas.problem: Every airline is supposed to mutilate parts that are beyond economical repair or time-expired so they cannot re-enter the supply chain. On the floor, the scrap cage gets emptied by a metals dealer on a handshake. Serial plates are sometimes cut off and sometimes not.
