Techs and stores people know that 'scrapped' units can turn up months later 'overhauled' at a broker with a tidy set of documents. The airline also carries the paper trail risk. If a fake part traces back to your serial number, you are in the investigation. Meanwhile titanium and nickel-alloy scrap is sold mixed at a low commodity price, because nobody segregates it.
ideas.solution: A van with a shear or plasma cutter, a tag punch and a phone app. Per drum or per pallet, the crew scans and photographs part number and serial number before destruction, destroys the part in a way that defeats reuse, photographs it again after, and pushes a hash-stamped certificate of destruction into the customer's inventory system. This removes the item from their books and gives quality staff and lessor auditors an unbroken chain of custody. Scrap is segregated by alloy and sold to specialty metal buyers, which funds the service.
ideas.why_now: Scrutiny of unapproved and counterfeit parts has stayed high since the 2023 forged-release-certificate scandal involving CFM56 parts. The FAA has long-standing guidance on detecting and reporting suspected unapproved parts (AC 21-29), and lessors and insurers keep tightening audit requirements. Fleet retirements of older regional aircraft in 2025-2026 are creating unusually large scrap volumes. Cheap phone-based photo and OCR capture removes the need for special hardware.
ideas.revenue_model: Fee per destruction event or per kilogram ($X per event plus a metal revenue share, typically netting near zero out of pocket for the airline). Annual chain-of-custody programs for lessors and MROs. Later, sell certified segregated alloy lots to aerospace melters at a premium.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Airlines treat scrap as a solved cost center. Techs know it is the weakest link in traceability. The buyer's pain is not the cost of scrap, it is being named in the paper trail of a counterfeit. Whoever owns certified destruction owns a record that every auditor, lessor and regulator increasingly wants. The metal value pays for the service, so the airline's out-of-pocket is close to zero, and that removes the budget objection.
ideas.first_30_days: Choose one metro with a regional hub plus several 145 shops. Buy a used band saw or plasma cutter and a tag punch, and line up a metals dealer that will accept segregated alloys. Have an aviation attorney draft a certificate of destruction that cites the operator's own manual procedure and AC 21-29. Offer the first scrap-cage clear-out free to 3-5 quality managers, with before and after photos and a metal check. Ask two lessor technical reps for introductions, since they carry the bigger volume.

ideas.title: Special-Tool Exchange for Retiring Regional Fleets
ideas.one_liner: Buy or take on consignment the OEM special tooling stranded when regionals retire 50-seat jets and older turboprops, calibrate it, and rent or sell it to operators who cannot get it from the OEM for months.
ideas.customer: MROs and Part 145 shops adding a regional-jet or turboprop type, Part 135 and cargo operators, freighter-conversion programs, and operators in Latin America, Africa and Asia flying older regional types. Sellers are regional airlines and lessors with tooling cages to empty.
ideas.problem: Every type needs OEM special tooling: rigging pins, wing and gear jack adapters, engine sling adapters, pinning tools, pressure-test rigs, borescope adapters, prop and control-rigging fixtures. New from the OEM this is expensive and lead times can run to months, and some tooling is out of production. When a regional retires a subfleet, that tooling is on the tool-control ledger at near-zero book value, taking up cage space. It gets scrapped, shipped out with airframes, or forgotten. Buyers who are desperate for it have no idea the seller exists, and vice versa.
ideas.solution: A consignment marketplace and rental pool. Take tooling in from retiring fleets at no cash outlay, on a 70/30 split of sales and rentals. Inspect it, get it recalibrated through a metrology lab, tag it with a certificate, and catalog it with photos and drawing references. Rent it weekly or monthly with a deposit and freight, or sell it. Offer starter tooling bundles for a shop taking on a new type, such as everything needed for a first C-check on that airframe.
ideas.why_now: Majors keep replacing 50-seat regional jets and older turboprops with larger regional aircraft, so tooling cages empty every quarter. Cargo conversions and second-life operators in emerging markets are keeping the old types flying. OEM lead times and parts availability have been poor across the industry since 2022, so buyers will pay to skip the wait.
ideas.revenue_model: Consignment split on sales, rental fees at roughly 3-6% of replacement value per month, calibration and freight margin, and bundle pricing for new-type start-ups. Later, a subscription for shops that want guaranteed access to a tooling pool.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Tooling has none of the obsolescence problem of parts. It does not expire except for calibration. A directors of maintenance would rather give it away than pay to store it, and nobody knows who the buyers are. The unusual thing about this business is that the inventory is almost free and the demand is urgent, because a missing pin can ground an airplane for weeks.
ideas.first_30_days: Call 20 directors of maintenance, tech-services managers and lessor technical reps whose subfleets are winding down. Get two or three tool cages on consignment with no upfront cash. Photograph and catalog them, send calibrated items to a local metrology lab, and publish a simple catalog with rental terms and a deposit process. Contact freighter-conversion programs, Part 135 operators and international MROs that fly the same type. The first rental should close within weeks, because the urgency price is high.

ideas.title: NFC Open-Item Tags for Aircraft Shift Handover
ideas.one_liner: Tamper-evident NFC red-tags that record every opened panel, disconnected line and removed component on an aircraft, and block sign-off until each is closed with an as-left photo.
ideas.customer: Directors of maintenance, quality and safety managers at regional airlines, Part 145 shops, Part 135 fleets and helicopter EMS operators. Line stations with 3-6 techs per shift are the beachhead.
ideas.problem: The most dangerous moments in line maintenance are shift change and interruption. A tech opens a panel, disconnects a connector or leaves a cap loose, gets pulled to an AOG, and hands over verbally or with a sticky note. The 'system' is a paper red tag, a whiteboard and memory. The 2024 737 MAX 9 door-plug investigation put undocumented removal of fasteners in front of every director of maintenance. Digital task cards do not fix this, because the physical state of the aircraft between task steps is not captured anywhere.
ideas.solution: Tamper-evident NFC tags that hang on the physical thing that is open. A tech taps the tag with a phone (offline-first, because hangars have dead zones), records what, why and who, and hangs it. At handover, the app shows a manifest of open tags by tail. The aircraft cannot be released in the app until every tag is closed with an as-left photo. Export goes to the work order as PDF or CSV on day one, and to the maintenance system through an API later. Techs get a time-stamped record of exactly what they did and left.
ideas.why_now: The 2024 door-plug event made undocumented maintenance a board-level topic. The FAA's 2024 SMS final rule expanded safety-management obligations to more operators, and safety departments are looking for concrete evidence-capture tools. NFC-capable phones are standard and cheap tags are commodity, so the hardware cost is pennies. AI is a minor part of this, which is a feature. It ships without data-science risk.
ideas.revenue_model: Per-aircraft subscription ($75-150 per tail per month) plus consumable tags at $0.50-1.50 each, the razor-and-blade model that made lockout-tagout a large industrial category. Enterprise tier with maintenance-system integration and safety analytics.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Maintenance software dies at the tech's hands, because anything that adds keystrokes gets skipped. This replaces a paper red tag with something faster, and it gives the tech a personal alibi for their own certificate if something is questioned years later. The buyer is quality and safety, not IT, so it needs no integration with the maintenance system to start. Underneath the software is a consumables business.
ideas.first_30_days: Ask your own director of maintenance to pilot it at your line station, so you can test it during real shift changes. Build a progressive web app with offline storage and buy 2,000 off-the-shelf NFC stickers. Run a free 30-day pilot at two line stations and one Part 145 shop, then measure tags closed with photo, handover time and missed items caught. Convert the pilot to $99 per tail per month plus tags, and use the measured near-misses as the sales collateral for safety managers.

ideas.title: Airline-Grade Depot Maintenance for Drone Fleets
ideas.one_liner: A swap-based depot and records service that applies airline maintenance discipline to police drone-as-first-responder, ag-spray and utility inspection fleets.
ideas.customer: Sheriff's offices and municipal police and fire departments running 5-30 docked drones, agricultural spray operators, and utility and rail inspection contractors. The buyer is the program manager or operations lead, paying per airframe per month.
ideas.problem: Drone programs are run by one enthusiastic officer or a few pilots. Flying is the easy part. The real risks are battery cycle counts and swelling, motor and prop wear, firmware drift across a fleet, undocumented crash repairs, and no clear rule for when an aircraft is airworthy enough to dispatch. Aircraft techs recognize all of it: life-limited parts, configuration control, intermittent faults, 'no fault found', and sign-off traceability. Agencies also need records that survive scrutiny in court or after an incident. Manufacturer service plans cover their own hardware only and are mostly warranty repair, not fleet discipline.
ideas.solution: A monthly airframe subscription that includes a rotable-style exchange pool. When something fails, we ship an airworthy replacement airframe, gimbal or battery set overnight and take the broken one to our bench, so the program is never down. We keep per-airframe and per-battery records with QR codes, cycle counts and firmware baselines. We run a pre-deployment inspection checklist that acts like a simple minimum-equipment list for dispatch. Records are exported in evidentiary format. Techs staffing the bench are retired or moonlighting A&Ps.
ideas.why_now: The 2025 White House drone executive order and the FAA's proposed BVLOS rule (Part 108) point toward large fleets flying beyond visual line of sight, and hundreds of US police and fire departments are standing up drone-as-first-responder programs. Tightening US restrictions on Chinese-made drone equipment mean installed fleets must be kept flying for years while spare parts get scarce, which makes maintenance skill a moat. Mechanic supply is also loosening at the edges as retired A&Ps look for part-time work.
ideas.revenue_model: $450-900 per airframe per month for the exchange and records subscription, fixed-fee inspections ($150 per airframe), battery-audit fees, parts margin on refurbished airframes, and later a training and certification product for agency pilots.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Drone programs will relearn every airline lesson, and the money is in configuration control and records, not in flying. A rotable exchange pool beats field repair because the customer's real pain is downtime and liability, not the repair cost. Manufacturers mostly sell to fleets of one brand, but real fleets are multi-vendor, so an independent depot with an airline-style record system has room to win.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro and sign three agencies or ag operators to a discounted pilot at $450 per airframe per month. Set up a bench in a rented hangar bay or garage with two part-time A&Ps. Run the record system on Airtable with QR labels, and sell battery-health audits and pre-deployment inspections at fixed prices as the first paid products. Use an airline-style monthly 'fleet status' report as the marketing piece. By day 30, the target is at least one signed agreement and a small exchange pool of two spare airframes.
